u:core-dbms-61-log-based-recovery.title: Log-based recovery
u:core-dbms-61-log-based-recovery.summary: Write intentions to a log before changing data, so a crash can be undone or redone.

blocks.text: **Log-based recovery** uses a **write-ahead log (WAL)** — a sequential record of every change — to restore a consistent state after a crash. The **WAL rule**: a change's log record must reach stable storage **before** the change itself is written to the database.

items: Each log record holds: transaction id, data item, **old value** (for undo), **new value** (for redo).
**Undo** rolls back uncommitted transactions (using old values); **redo** re-applies committed ones (using new values).
Recovery scans the log to decide, per transaction, whether to undo or redo.

blocks.text: The WAL rule is what makes atomicity + durability possible: because the log records the intent before the data changes, a crash at any point can be recovered — undo the unfinished, redo the committed.
Deferred update writes changes only at commit (redo only); immediate update writes as it goes (needs undo and redo).

mcqs.q: The write-ahead logging (WAL) rule requires that:
options: Data is written before the log
The log record is written to stable storage before the corresponding data change
mcqs.explain: Logging the intent first ensures recovery can undo/redo after any crash.

mcqs.q: During recovery, committed transactions are:
mcqs.explain: Committed changes must be redone to ensure durability; uncommitted ones are undone.

mcqs.q: A log record typically stores, for undo/redo:
options: The old value and the new value of the data item
mcqs.explain: Old value enables undo; new value enables redo.

u:core-dbms-62-undo-and-redo.title: Undo and redo
u:core-dbms-62-undo-and-redo.summary: Two log operations: reverse the unfinished, replay the finished.

blocks.text: Recovery applies two operations based on the log.

rows: Committed transactions whose changes may not have reached disk

blocks.text: A transaction is **redone** if the log has both its start and its **commit** record; it's **undone** if it started but has no commit. To be safe, recovery typically **redoes then undoes** (or vice versa depending on the algorithm), and operations must be **idempotent** so re-running recovery is safe.

The rule: has a commit record → REDO (restore durability); no commit record → UNDO (restore atomicity). Idempotency means applying redo/undo twice has the same effect as once — vital if recovery itself is interrupted.

mcqs.q: A transaction with a start but NO commit record in the log is:
mcqs.explain: No commit means it was in-flight at the crash, so it must be undone to preserve atomicity.

mcqs.q: REDO uses which values to reapply changes?
mcqs.explain: Redo re-applies the committed new values to ensure durability.

mcqs.q: Undo/redo operations must be idempotent so that:
options: Re-running recovery (e.g. after a second crash) is safe
mcqs.explain: Idempotency lets recovery be safely repeated if it is itself interrupted.

u:core-dbms-63-checkpoints.title: Checkpoints
u:core-dbms-63-checkpoints.summary: Periodic sync points that bound how much of the log recovery must scan.

blocks.text: Without help, recovery would have to scan the **entire** log from the beginning. A **checkpoint** is a point at which the DBMS flushes in-memory changes to disk and writes a checkpoint record, so recovery only needs to consider work **after** the last checkpoint.

items: At a checkpoint: flush the log and modified buffers to disk, and record the list of active transactions.
Recovery starts from the last checkpoint, not the log's start — bounding recovery time.
Transactions that committed before the checkpoint need no redo.

blocks.text: Checkpoints bound recovery work: after a crash, only transactions active at or after the last checkpoint matter. This trades a small runtime cost (periodic flushing) for a much shorter, predictable recovery.

mcqs.q: The purpose of a checkpoint is to:
options: Limit how far back recovery must scan the log
mcqs.explain: Checkpoints let recovery start from a recent point instead of the log's beginning, bounding recovery time.

mcqs.q: At a checkpoint, the DBMS:
options: Flushes in-memory changes/log to disk and records active transactions
mcqs.explain: It persists buffers and the log and notes which transactions are active, creating a known-good reference point.

mcqs.q: A transaction that committed BEFORE the last checkpoint:
mcqs.explain: Its changes were flushed at the checkpoint, so redo isn't needed.

u:core-dbms-64-shadow-paging.title: Shadow paging
u:core-dbms-64-shadow-paging.summary: A log-free recovery scheme using a shadow copy of the page table.

blocks.text: **Shadow paging** is an alternative to logging. It keeps two page tables: the **current** (shadow) page table and a working copy. Modified pages are written to **new** pages (copy-on-write), not overwritten. On **commit**, the page table is atomically switched to point at the new pages; to **abort**, just discard the new pages and keep the shadow.

items: **No undo/redo log** needed — the old version survives untouched until commit.
Commit = atomically switch the page-table pointer.
Downsides: **fragmentation** and **garbage collection** of old pages; hard to support **concurrent** transactions; extra copying.

blocks.text: Shadow paging trades the log for copy-on-write: recovery is trivial (revert to the shadow), but it fragments storage, needs garbage collection, and doesn't handle concurrency well — which is why WAL/logging dominates in practice.

mcqs.q: Shadow paging avoids the need for a(n):
mcqs.explain: By keeping an untouched shadow copy, recovery reverts to it without a log.

mcqs.q: In shadow paging, committing a transaction means:
options: Atomically switching the page table to the new pages
mcqs.explain: The page-table pointer switch atomically makes the new pages current; abort discards them.

mcqs.q: A major drawback of shadow paging is:
options: Fragmentation, garbage collection, and poor concurrency support
mcqs.explain: Copy-on-write scatters pages and complicates GC and concurrency, so logging is usually preferred.

u:core-dbms-65-aries-at-a-high-level.title: ARIES at a high level
u:core-dbms-65-aries-at-a-high-level.summary: The industry-standard recovery algorithm: analysis, redo everything, then undo the losers.

blocks.text: **ARIES** is the widely-used recovery algorithm (in DB2, SQL Server, etc.). It's built on **WAL** and a key principle: **redo history** (repeat all logged actions), then undo the uncommitted. It uses a **Log Sequence Number (LSN)** on every log record and page.
Three phases

items: **Analysis** — scan forward from the last checkpoint to find dirty pages and transactions active at the crash.
**Redo** — replay ALL changes since the relevant point (even uncommitted ones) to restore the exact pre-crash page state ('repeating history').
**Undo** — roll back the transactions that were uncommitted at the crash, writing **compensation log records (CLRs)** so undo itself is recoverable.

blocks.text: ARIES's signature ideas: WAL + LSNs to track what's on each page, 'repeat history' in redo (reconstruct exact state), and CLRs so that a crash during recovery doesn't undo work twice.

mcqs.q: The three phases of ARIES recovery, in order, are:
mcqs.explain: ARIES runs Analysis (find state), then Redo (repeat history), then Undo (roll back losers).

mcqs.q: ARIES's 'repeat history' principle means the redo phase:
options: Replays all logged changes to restore the exact pre-crash state
mcqs.explain: Redo reconstructs the precise state at crash time (including uncommitted changes), which undo then cleans up.

mcqs.q: Compensation Log Records (CLRs) in ARIES ensure that:
options: Undo actions are logged so recovery is idempotent even if it crashes again
mcqs.explain: CLRs record undo work so a crash during undo doesn't cause it to be repeated incorrectly.

u:core-dbms-66-dense-vs-sparse-index.title: Dense vs sparse index
u:core-dbms-66-dense-vs-sparse-index.summary: An index entry for every record, or one per block — space vs lookup trade-off.

blocks.text: An **index** maps search-key values to record locations for fast lookup. Two structures differ in how many entries they keep.

rows: One per block (usually the first key)
Direct — key found in the index
Find the block, then scan within it

blocks.text: Dense = an entry per record (bigger index, direct lookup); sparse = an entry per block (smaller index, but the data must be sorted and you scan within the block). Sparse indexes save space, which is why they're used at upper levels of multilevel indexes.
A primary (clustering) index on sorted data can be sparse; a secondary index on unsorted data must be dense.

mcqs.q: A dense index has:
options: One index entry for every record (search-key value)
mcqs.explain: Dense indexes store an entry per record, enabling direct key lookup at the cost of size.

mcqs.q: A sparse index requires that the data file is:
mcqs.explain: Because it stores one entry per block, the records must be ordered so a block scan finds the key.

mcqs.q: A secondary index on an unsorted attribute must be:
mcqs.explain: Without ordering on that key, you can't rely on block scanning, so every record needs an entry (dense).

u:core-dbms-67-primary-clustered-seconda.title: Primary, clustered, secondary index
u:core-dbms-67-primary-clustered-seconda.summary: Indexes classified by whether they dictate physical row order.

blocks.text: Indexes are classified by their relationship to the physical storage order.

items: **Clustered index** — the table's rows are physically stored in the index's order. There can be **only one** per table (data can be sorted one way). Range scans are very fast.
**Primary index** — a clustered index on the ordering key (often the primary key).
**Secondary (non-clustered) index** — a separate structure pointing to rows; the table order is unaffected. A table can have **many**. Lookups need an extra step to fetch the row.

blocks.text: Clustered = data IS the index (one per table, fast ranges). Non-clustered/secondary = a pointer structure (many per table, extra hop to the row). Choosing the clustered key wisely (often the most range-queried column) matters a lot for performance.
In many DBs the primary key becomes the clustered index by default; a non-clustered index lookup does a 'key lookup' back into the clustered index to get remaining columns.

mcqs.q: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
mcqs.explain: A clustered index defines the physical row order, and data can only be ordered one way — so at most one per table.

mcqs.q: A secondary (non-clustered) index:
options: Is a separate structure pointing to rows; a table can have many
mcqs.explain: Non-clustered indexes don't affect table order and there can be several, each pointing to the underlying rows.

mcqs.q: Clustered indexes make which operation especially fast?
options: Range scans (rows stored contiguously in key order)
mcqs.explain: Because rows are physically ordered by the key, range queries read contiguous data efficiently.

u:core-dbms-68-b-tree.title: B-tree
u:core-dbms-68-b-tree.summary: A balanced multi-way search tree that keeps disk lookups shallow and logarithmic.

blocks.text: A **B-tree** is a self-balancing search tree where each node holds **many keys** and has **many children** (high fanout), so the tree stays **shallow**. This minimises disk I/O: each node is a disk block, and a shallow tree means few block reads per lookup.

items: All leaves are at the **same depth** (balanced), so every lookup is O(log n) with a small base (high fanout).
Keys (and their data pointers) can live in **internal nodes** as well as leaves.
Supports search, sequential access, insert, and delete in logarithmic time; nodes split/merge to stay balanced.

blocks.text: The reason databases use B-trees over binary trees: high fanout keeps the tree shallow, so a lookup touches only a handful of disk blocks. Disk I/O, not comparisons, is the cost that matters.

mcqs.q: Databases favour B-trees over binary search trees because B-trees:
options: Have high fanout, keeping the tree shallow and minimising disk I/O
mcqs.explain: Many keys per node means fewer levels, so far fewer disk block reads per lookup.

mcqs.q: In a B-tree, all leaf nodes are:
mcqs.explain: B-trees are height-balanced, so every root-to-leaf path has the same length.

mcqs.q: In a B-tree (not B+), data pointers can be stored:
options: In both internal nodes and leaves
mcqs.explain: A B-tree stores keys and pointers throughout, unlike a B+ tree which keeps data only in leaves.

u:core-dbms-69-b-tree-and-why-dbs-prefer.title: B+ tree and why DBs prefer it
u:core-dbms-69-b-tree-and-why-dbs-prefer.summary: Data only in leaves, with linked leaves — the near-universal database index structure.

blocks.text: A **B+ tree** is a B-tree variant where **all data pointers live in the leaf nodes** and internal nodes hold only keys for routing. The leaves are also **linked** in a sequential chain.
Why databases prefer B+ trees

items: Internal nodes store **only keys** (no data), so each holds **more keys** → **higher fanout** → an even **shallower** tree → fewer disk reads.
**Linked leaves** make **range queries** and ordered scans very efficient — find the start, then walk the leaf chain.
Predictable performance: every lookup goes all the way to a leaf (uniform path length).

blocks.text: B+ tree wins on two fronts: keys-only internal nodes give higher fanout (shallower tree, less I/O), and the linked leaf level makes range scans a simple sequential walk. That's why it's the default index in virtually every RDBMS.

mcqs.q: In a B+ tree, data record pointers are stored:
mcqs.explain: B+ trees keep data only in leaves; internal nodes hold keys purely for navigation.

mcqs.q: B+ trees make range queries efficient because:
options: Leaves are linked in a sequential chain to scan in order
mcqs.explain: The linked leaf level lets a range scan find the start and walk sequentially through the leaves.

mcqs.q: Keeping data out of internal nodes gives a B+ tree:
options: Higher fanout and a shallower tree (fewer disk reads)
mcqs.explain: Keys-only internal nodes pack more keys per node, raising fanout and reducing tree height.

u:core-dbms-70-hash-indexing-static-dyna.title: Hash indexing: static, dynamic, extendible
u:core-dbms-70-hash-indexing-static-dyna.summary: Constant-time equality lookups via hashing — and how to grow buckets without full rehash.

blocks.text: **Hash indexing** maps a search key through a hash function to a **bucket**, giving **O(1)** average lookup for **equality** searches (but no range support).

rows: Fixed number of buckets; overflow chains when full → degrades
A directory doubles; only the overflowing bucket splits (no full rehash)
Buckets split one at a time in a fixed order as the file grows

blocks.text: Hash indexes give O(1) equality lookups but **can't do range queries** (hashing scatters order) — that's the key trade-off vs B+ trees. Extendible/linear hashing avoid the static-hashing problem of rehashing everything when buckets overflow.
Because hashing destroys ordering, use B+ trees for range/sort queries and hash indexes only for exact-match lookups.

mcqs.q: A hash index is unsuitable for:
options: Range queries (e.g. WHERE x BETWEEN a AND b)
mcqs.explain: Hashing scatters keys, destroying order, so range scans aren't supported — unlike B+ trees.

mcqs.q: Extendible hashing avoids rehashing all data by:
options: Using a directory that doubles and splitting only the overflowing bucket
mcqs.explain: It grows the directory and splits just the full bucket, avoiding a full-file rehash.

mcqs.q: The average lookup time for an equality search in a good hash index is:
mcqs.explain: Hashing gives constant average-time equality lookups.

u:core-dbms-71-covering-index.title: Covering index
u:core-dbms-71-covering-index.summary: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the table itself is never touched.

blocks.text: A **covering index** includes all the columns a query references (in the key or as **included** columns), so the query can be answered **entirely from the index** — no lookup back to the table (an 'index-only scan').

items: Normally a non-clustered index lookup fetches matching keys, then does a **key/bookmark lookup** into the table for other columns — an extra I/O per row.
If the index already contains those columns, that second step is eliminated — a big speedup for hot queries.
Built by adding columns to the index (as key or INCLUDE columns).

blocks.text: A covering index 'covers' a query: SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN columns are all in the index, so the engine never reads the base table. It trades extra index size/write cost for faster reads.

mcqs.q: A covering index speeds up a query by:
options: Containing all needed columns so the table isn't accessed (index-only scan)
mcqs.explain: If the index has every column the query needs, the engine answers it from the index alone, skipping table lookups.

mcqs.q: Without a covering index, a non-clustered index lookup often requires:
options: A key/bookmark lookup into the base table for remaining columns
mcqs.explain: The index gives the location; extra columns require an additional fetch from the table.

mcqs.q: The cost of a covering index is:
options: Larger index size and higher write/update overhead
mcqs.explain: Including more columns enlarges the index and adds maintenance cost on writes.

u:core-dbms-72-when-an-index-hurts.title: When an index hurts
u:core-dbms-72-when-an-index-hurts.summary: Indexes aren't free — they slow writes and can be ignored or counterproductive.

blocks.text: Indexes speed reads but have costs. Knowing when NOT to index shows real understanding.

items: **Write overhead** — every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update every index on the table. Many indexes = slow writes.
**Low selectivity** — an index on a column with few distinct values (e.g. a boolean/gender) is often useless; the optimiser prefers a full scan.
**Small tables** — scanning is cheaper than an index lookup.
**Storage** — indexes consume disk and memory.
**Functions on the column** — `WHERE UPPER(name) = ...` can't use a plain index on name (unless a functional index exists).

blocks.text: Index for read patterns, not reflexively. On write-heavy tables, low-selectivity columns, or small tables, an index can cost more than it saves. Wrapping an indexed column in a function also disables the index.

mcqs.q: An index generally hurts performance when the table is:
options: Write-heavy (each write must update the index too)
mcqs.explain: Every write maintains every index, so many indexes slow inserts/updates/deletes.

mcqs.q: An index on a low-selectivity column (few distinct values) is often:
options: Ignored by the optimiser in favour of a full scan
mcqs.explain: When most rows share a value, a scan is cheaper than using the index.

mcqs.q: `WHERE UPPER(name) = 'X'` typically:
options: Uses a plain index on name
Cannot use a plain index on name (function applied to the column)
mcqs.explain: Applying a function to the column prevents use of a normal index unless a matching functional index exists.

u:core-dbms-73-query-plans-and-explain.title: Query plans and EXPLAIN
u:core-dbms-73-query-plans-and-explain.summary: See how the database will run a query, and spot the slow parts.

blocks.text: The **query optimiser** turns your SQL into an **execution plan** — the concrete steps (which indexes, join methods, order). `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`) shows this plan so you can diagnose performance.

items: **Access methods**: full **table scan** (read everything) vs **index scan/seek** (use an index).
**Join methods**: nested loop (good for small/indexed), hash join (large unsorted sets), merge join (both sorted).
Watch for a full scan on a large table, a huge estimated **row count** mismatch (stale statistics), or a missing index.
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and shows actual timings/rows vs estimates.

blocks.text: EXPLAIN reveals whether the DB uses your index, how it joins, and where the cost is. The most common finding is a full table scan where an index would help, or bad estimates from stale statistics.

mcqs.q: EXPLAIN is used to:
options: Show the query's execution plan without (or with) running it
mcqs.explain: EXPLAIN reveals the optimiser's chosen plan so you can analyse performance.

mcqs.q: A common performance red flag in a plan is:
options: A full table scan on a large table where an index would help
mcqs.explain: Scanning a big table instead of using an index usually signals a missing/unused index.

mcqs.q: A hash join is typically chosen for:
mcqs.explain: Hash joins suit large unsorted inputs; nested loops fit small/indexed inputs and merge joins fit sorted inputs.

u:core-dbms-74-sql-vs-nosql-trade-offs.title: SQL vs NoSQL trade-offs
u:core-dbms-74-sql-vs-nosql-trade-offs.summary: Structured, consistent, relational vs flexible, scalable, denormalized — choose by need.

blocks.text: SQL (relational) and NoSQL databases make different trade-offs; the right choice depends on the workload.

rows: High scale, flexible/varied data, simple access patterns

blocks.text: Pick SQL for structured data needing strong consistency, complex queries, and transactions (finance, orders). Pick NoSQL for massive scale, flexible/evolving schemas, or specific access patterns (feeds, catalogs, sessions). It's about fit, not one being 'better'.
Modern systems are often polyglot: relational for core transactional data, NoSQL for caching, search, feeds, or analytics.

mcqs.q: A key strength of relational (SQL) databases is:
options: Strong consistency (ACID) and complex query/join support
mcqs.explain: SQL databases excel at structured data, transactions, and complex queries with joins.

mcqs.q: NoSQL databases are typically chosen for:
mcqs.explain: NoSQL targets scale and schema flexibility, often trading some consistency and join capability.

mcqs.q: The choice between SQL and NoSQL should be based on:
options: The workload's needs (consistency, scale, query complexity, schema)
mcqs.explain: It's a fit-for-purpose decision driven by data structure, consistency, scale, and query needs.

u:core-dbms-75-document-key-value-column.title: Document, key-value, column, graph stores
u:core-dbms-75-document-key-value-column.summary: The four main NoSQL families, each tuned to a data shape and access pattern.

blocks.text: NoSQL isn't one thing — it's four families, each optimised for a different data model.

Match the store to the shape: key-value for simple fast lookups, document for flexible self-contained records, wide-column for massive scale, graph for relationship-heavy queries (friends-of-friends, paths).

mcqs.q: Which NoSQL type is best for highly connected data like social networks?
mcqs.explain: Graph databases model nodes and edges directly, making relationship traversals (e.g. friends-of-friends) efficient.

mcqs.q: A key-value store like Redis is ideal for:
options: Fast simple lookups such as caching and sessions
mcqs.explain: Key-value stores give very fast get/set on a key, suiting caches and session storage.

mcqs.q: A document store (e.g. MongoDB) organises data as:
options: Rows and columns with fixed schema
Flexible JSON/BSON documents keyed by id
mcqs.explain: Document databases store semi-structured documents, allowing flexible, self-contained records.

u:core-dbms-76-cap-theorem.title: CAP theorem
u:core-dbms-76-cap-theorem.summary: In a network partition, a distributed store can guarantee consistency or availability, not both.

blocks.text: The **CAP theorem** states a distributed data store can provide at most **two** of: **Consistency** (every read sees the latest write), **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response), **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps working despite network splits).
Since network **partitions are unavoidable** in real distributed systems, P is mandatory. So the real choice during a partition is **C vs A**:

rows: Stay available, may return stale data

blocks.text: The real meaning: because partitions happen, you must choose — during a partition, be **consistent** (CP: refuse to serve possibly-stale data) or **available** (AP: serve, accepting staleness). 'Pick 2 of 3' is really 'pick C or A when P occurs'.
PACELC refines CAP: else (when no partition), you still trade Latency vs Consistency. See the PACELC note in the System Design pack.

mcqs.q: The CAP theorem says a distributed store, during a network partition, must choose between:
mcqs.explain: Partition tolerance is required, so the trade-off during a partition is consistency vs availability.

mcqs.q: A CP system during a partition will:
options: Sacrifice availability to remain consistent (reject/block some requests)
mcqs.explain: CP systems prioritise consistency, refusing to serve data they can't guarantee is current.

mcqs.q: An AP system like Cassandra during a partition:
options: Stays available but may return stale (eventually consistent) data
mcqs.explain: AP systems keep answering requests, accepting temporary inconsistency (eventual consistency).

u:core-dbms-77-sharding-and-replication.title: Sharding and replication
u:core-dbms-77-sharding-and-replication.summary: Split data across nodes for write scale; copy data across nodes for reads and resilience.

blocks.text: Two orthogonal techniques for scaling a distributed database — often confused, usually combined.

items: **Sharding (partitioning)** — split data into subsets, each on a different node, by a **shard key** (range or hash). Scales **writes** and **storage**; each node handles part of the load.
**Replication** — keep **copies** of the same data on multiple nodes. Scales **reads** and provides **availability/failover**; replicas can lag (eventual consistency).

blocks.text: Sharding = different data on different nodes (write/storage scale); replication = same data copied (read scale + fault tolerance). Large systems shard AND replicate each shard. Choosing a good shard key (to avoid hotspots) is the hard part.
Cross-shard queries and transactions are expensive and complex — a major reason to choose the shard key so that most queries hit a single shard.

mcqs.q: Sharding primarily scales:
options: Writes and storage, by splitting data across nodes
mcqs.explain: Each shard holds a subset of the data, distributing write and storage load.

mcqs.q: Replication primarily provides:
options: Read scaling and availability via copies of the same data
mcqs.explain: Copies let reads spread across replicas and provide failover if a node dies.

mcqs.q: A poorly chosen shard key leads to:
options: Hotspots (one shard overloaded) and costly cross-shard queries
mcqs.explain: A bad key concentrates load on one shard and forces expensive cross-shard operations.

u:core-dbms-78-normalisation-vs-denormal.title: Normalisation vs denormalisation in practice
u:core-dbms-78-normalisation-vs-denormal.summary: The real-world balance: normalize for integrity, denormalize selectively for read speed.

blocks.text: In practice you don't pick one dogmatically — you normalize as the default and denormalize deliberately where measured performance demands it.

Rule of thumb: normalize for **OLTP** (transactional integrity, many writes), denormalize for **OLAP/reporting** (read-heavy analytics, star schemas). Denormalize only after measuring that joins are the bottleneck — and then manage the consistency cost.
Common hybrid: keep a normalized source of truth, and maintain denormalized read models / materialized views / caches for hot read paths.

mcqs.q: Transactional (OLTP) systems generally favour:
options: Normalisation for integrity and consistent writes
mcqs.explain: OLTP prioritises write consistency and integrity, which normalisation provides.

mcqs.q: Denormalisation is most appropriate for:
mcqs.explain: Analytics/reporting benefit from precomputed, join-free data at the cost of write complexity.

mcqs.q: A common practical hybrid is to:
options: Keep a normalized source of truth plus denormalized read models/materialized views for hot reads
mcqs.explain: A normalized core with maintained denormalized read paths balances integrity and read speed.

u:core-dbms-48-acid-properties.title: ACID properties
u:core-dbms-48-acid-properties.summary: The four guarantees that make a transaction reliable: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

blocks.text: A **transaction** is a unit of work that must execute completely or not at all. **ACID** is the set of guarantees that make transactions reliable.

rows: All operations happen, or none do (all-or-nothing; rollback on failure)
A transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another (constraints hold)
Concurrent transactions don't interfere; result as if run serially
Once committed, changes survive crashes (persisted to disk/log)

blocks.text: Classic example: a bank transfer. Atomicity ensures the debit and credit both happen or neither; Consistency keeps total money constant; Isolation stops another transaction seeing a half-done transfer; Durability keeps it after a crash.
Atomicity is enabled by the log (undo); Durability by the log (redo) + write-ahead logging; Isolation by concurrency control (locks/MVCC).

mcqs.q: Atomicity guarantees that a transaction:
options: Executes fully or not at all (all-or-nothing)
mcqs.explain: Atomicity means all operations commit together or none do — partial effects are rolled back.

mcqs.q: Durability ensures that once a transaction commits:
options: Its changes persist even after a system crash
mcqs.explain: Committed changes are made permanent (via logging), surviving failures.

mcqs.q: The property preventing concurrent transactions from seeing each other's uncommitted changes is:
mcqs.explain: Isolation makes concurrent transactions behave as if serialized, hiding intermediate states.

u:core-dbms-49-transaction-states.title: Transaction states
u:core-dbms-49-transaction-states.summary: The lifecycle of a transaction from active through committed or aborted.

blocks.text: A transaction moves through a defined set of **states**.

items: **Active** — executing its operations.
**Partially committed** — after the final operation, before changes are made permanent.
**Committed** — changes durably saved; the transaction succeeded.
**Failed** — an error occurred; normal execution can't continue.
**Aborted** — rolled back to the state before it started (may be restarted).

blocks.text: The two terminal outcomes are **committed** (permanent) and **aborted** (rolled back). 'Partially committed' is the risky window before durability is guaranteed — a crash here triggers recovery.

mcqs.q: After executing its last statement but before changes are made permanent, a transaction is:
mcqs.explain: Partially committed is the state between the final operation and durable commit.

mcqs.q: A transaction that fails and is rolled back to its start reaches the state:
mcqs.explain: After a failure, the transaction is aborted (undone) and may be restarted.

mcqs.q: The two terminal states of a transaction are:
mcqs.explain: A transaction ends either committed (success) or aborted (rolled back).

u:core-dbms-50-schedules-serial-non-seri.title: Schedules: serial, non-serial
u:core-dbms-50-schedules-serial-non-seri.summary: The order in which concurrent transactions' operations interleave.

blocks.text: A **schedule** is the chronological order of operations from multiple transactions.

items: **Serial schedule** — transactions run one completely before the next; always correct, but no concurrency (slow).
**Non-serial (concurrent) schedule** — operations interleave for performance, but may be incorrect if not equivalent to some serial order.
The goal of concurrency control: allow non-serial schedules that are **serializable** (equivalent to a serial one).

blocks.text: Serial schedules are always correct but slow; non-serial schedules are fast but must be **serializable** to be correct. Serializability is the correctness criterion that lets us have concurrency safely.

mcqs.q: A serial schedule executes transactions:
options: One entirely before the next begins
mcqs.explain: Serial means no interleaving — each transaction finishes before the next starts, guaranteeing correctness.

mcqs.q: Non-serial schedules are used because they:
options: Allow concurrency and better performance (if serializable)
mcqs.explain: Interleaving boosts throughput, but only serializable non-serial schedules are correct.

mcqs.q: The correctness goal for a concurrent schedule is that it is:
mcqs.explain: Serializability ensures a concurrent schedule yields the same result as some serial order.

u:core-dbms-51-conflict-serializability-.title: Conflict serializability and precedence graph
u:core-dbms-51-conflict-serializability-.summary: Test whether a schedule is equivalent to a serial one by checking its precedence graph for cycles.

blocks.text: Two operations **conflict** if they belong to different transactions, access the **same data item**, and at least one is a **write**. A schedule is **conflict serializable** if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping only non-conflicting operations.
The precedence graph test

items: Make a node per transaction.
Add an edge Ti to Tj whenever an operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes an operation of Tj on the same item.
The schedule is conflict serializable if and only if the graph has no cycle. A topological sort of an acyclic graph gives an equivalent serial order.

blocks.text: The whole test reduces to cycle detection: no cycle in the precedence (serializability) graph implies conflict serializable implies correct. A cycle means no equivalent serial order exists.
Conflict serializability is a sufficient (stricter) condition for correctness; view serializability is more permissive but harder (NP) to test.

mcqs.q: Two operations conflict when they are from different transactions, hit the same item, and:
options: At least one is a write
mcqs.explain: Read-write or write-write on the same item conflict; two reads do not.

mcqs.q: A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph:
mcqs.explain: No cycle means the operations can be topologically ordered into an equivalent serial schedule.

mcqs.q: An edge from Ti to Tj in the precedence graph means:
options: An operation of Ti conflicts with and precedes one of Tj
They read the same item only
mcqs.explain: The edge records that Ti must come before Tj in any equivalent serial order due to a conflict.

u:core-dbms-52-view-serializability.title: View serializability
u:core-dbms-52-view-serializability.summary: A broader correctness notion than conflict serializability, based on what each read sees.

blocks.text: **View serializability** is a weaker (more permissive) correctness criterion than conflict serializability. Two schedules are **view equivalent** if, for every data item, they agree on: initial reads, which write each read sees, and the final write.

items: Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable, but **not** vice versa.
View serializability additionally admits some schedules with **blind writes** (writing without reading first).
Testing view serializability is **NP-complete**, so practical systems enforce the cheaper conflict serializability.

blocks.text: Relationship: conflict serializable is a subset of view serializable. View serializability captures more valid schedules (those with blind writes) but is impractical to test (NP-complete), so real DBMSs use conflict serializability.

mcqs.q: Every conflict-serializable schedule is:
mcqs.explain: Conflict serializability is stricter, so it implies view serializability (but not conversely).

mcqs.q: View serializability admits some schedules that conflict serializability rejects, involving:
options: Blind writes (writing without a prior read)
mcqs.explain: Blind writes let certain view-serializable schedules exist that aren't conflict serializable.

mcqs.q: Practical systems use conflict serializability instead of view serializability because:
options: Testing view serializability is NP-complete (too expensive)
mcqs.explain: View serializability is hard (NP-complete) to check, so the efficiently-testable conflict serializability is enforced.

u:core-dbms-53-recoverable-and-cascadele.title: Recoverable and cascadeless schedules
u:core-dbms-53-recoverable-and-cascadele.summary: Rules on commit order and dirty reads so aborts don't corrupt other transactions.

blocks.text: Serializability isn't enough — schedules must also behave correctly when a transaction **aborts**.

items: **Recoverable** — a transaction commits only **after** every transaction whose data it read has committed. Otherwise, if the earlier one aborts, you've committed based on data that never existed.
**Cascadeless (avoids cascading rollback)** — a transaction reads only data written by **already-committed** transactions, so one abort never forces others to roll back.
**Strict** — even stronger: no transaction reads OR overwrites uncommitted data. Strict schedules simplify recovery.

blocks.text: The hierarchy: strict is a subset of cascadeless is a subset of recoverable. A **dirty read** (reading uncommitted data) is what makes a schedule non-cascadeless and risks cascading aborts. Strict 2PL produces strict schedules — no cascades.

mcqs.q: A recoverable schedule requires that a transaction commits only after:
options: Every transaction it read data from has committed
mcqs.explain: Committing after your data sources commit prevents relying on data that might be rolled back.

mcqs.q: A cascadeless schedule avoids cascading rollback by ensuring transactions read only:
mcqs.explain: Reading only committed data means one abort can't force others to roll back.

mcqs.q: A dirty read is:
options: Reading data written by an uncommitted transaction
mcqs.explain: A dirty read sees uncommitted changes, which can vanish if that transaction aborts.

u:core-dbms-54-lock-based-protocols.title: Lock-based protocols
u:core-dbms-54-lock-based-protocols.summary: Shared and exclusive locks control concurrent access to data items.

blocks.text: **Locking** is the most common concurrency-control mechanism. A transaction locks a data item before accessing it.

items: Many transactions can hold **S** locks on the same item simultaneously (concurrent reads are safe).
An **X** lock is exclusive — no other lock (S or X) can coexist.
The compatibility matrix: S-S compatible; S-X and X-X incompatible.

blocks.text: Shared locks allow concurrent reads; an exclusive lock is needed for writes and blocks everyone else. Locking alone doesn't guarantee serializability — you also need a protocol like 2PL governing when locks are acquired/released.

mcqs.q: Multiple transactions can simultaneously hold a shared (S) lock on the same item because:
mcqs.explain: Shared locks permit concurrent reading, which is safe; only writes need exclusivity.

mcqs.q: An exclusive (X) lock is compatible with:
mcqs.explain: An X lock must be held alone — it's incompatible with any other S or X lock.

mcqs.q: Locking by itself guarantees serializability:
options: No — it also needs a protocol like two-phase locking
mcqs.explain: Ad-hoc locking can still allow non-serializable schedules; a protocol like 2PL is required.

u:core-dbms-55-two-phase-locking-and-str.title: Two-phase locking and strict 2PL
u:core-dbms-55-two-phase-locking-and-str.summary: Acquire all locks before releasing any — the protocol that guarantees serializability.

blocks.text: **Two-Phase Locking (2PL)** guarantees conflict-serializable schedules by splitting a transaction's locking into two phases:

items: **Growing phase** — the transaction acquires locks; it may not release any.
**Shrinking phase** — once it releases its first lock, it may not acquire any more.
This 'all locks before any release' rule enforces serializability.

blocks.text: Variants

rows: Hold all X locks until commit/abort
No dirty reads / no cascading aborts
Hold ALL locks (S and X) until commit

blocks.text: 2PL guarantees serializability but can cause **deadlock** (two transactions each waiting for the other's lock). Strict 2PL, the most common in practice, holds exclusive locks until commit, avoiding cascading rollbacks.

mcqs.q: The two-phase locking rule is:
options: Release all locks before acquiring any
No lock is acquired after the first lock is released (growing then shrinking)
mcqs.explain: 2PL has a growing phase (acquire) then a shrinking phase (release); no acquisition after the first release.

mcqs.q: Strict 2PL additionally requires that exclusive locks are held:
options: Until the transaction commits or aborts
mcqs.explain: Holding X locks to commit prevents dirty reads and cascading rollbacks.

mcqs.q: A drawback of two-phase locking is that it can cause:
mcqs.explain: Transactions holding locks and waiting for each other's can deadlock; 2PL guarantees serializability but not deadlock-freedom.

u:core-dbms-56-isolation-levels.title: Isolation levels
u:core-dbms-56-isolation-levels.summary: Trade consistency for concurrency via four SQL levels, each permitting more anomalies.

blocks.text: **Isolation levels** let you relax full isolation for more concurrency, each allowing more read anomalies. The SQL standard defines four.

Higher isolation = fewer anomalies but less concurrency. Read Committed (the default in many DBs) prevents dirty reads; Serializable prevents everything but costs the most. Pick the lowest level that's still correct for your workload.
Many databases implement these with MVCC (snapshot isolation) rather than pure locking; snapshot isolation is close to but not exactly Serializable.

mcqs.q: Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
mcqs.explain: Only Read Uncommitted permits reading uncommitted (dirty) data; the others forbid it.

mcqs.q: Repeatable Read prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but may still allow:
mcqs.explain: Repeatable Read fixes existing rows but new rows matching a query (phantoms) can still appear.

mcqs.q: The trade-off of higher isolation levels is:
mcqs.explain: Stronger isolation reduces anomalies but limits concurrent execution, costing throughput.

u:core-dbms-57-dirty-read-non-repeatable.title: Dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read
u:core-dbms-57-dirty-read-non-repeatable.summary: The three concurrency anomalies isolation levels are designed to prevent.

blocks.text: These three read anomalies define what each isolation level allows.

items: **Dirty read** — reading data written by a transaction that hasn't committed (and might roll back). You read a value that never officially existed.
**Non-repeatable read** — reading the same **row** twice in one transaction and getting different values, because another transaction updated and committed it in between.
**Phantom read** — re-running the same **range query** returns a different set of rows, because another transaction inserted/deleted rows matching the condition.

blocks.text: The distinction: non-repeatable read is about a changed ROW value; phantom read is about the SET of rows changing (new/removed rows). Dirty read is about uncommitted data. Each is blocked by a progressively higher isolation level.

mcqs.q: Reading a value that a not-yet-committed transaction wrote is a:
mcqs.explain: A dirty read sees uncommitted data that may later be rolled back.

mcqs.q: Getting different values when reading the SAME row twice in a transaction is a:
mcqs.explain: A committed update by another transaction between the two reads causes a non-repeatable read.

mcqs.q: A phantom read specifically involves:
options: The set of rows matching a query changing (rows inserted/deleted)
mcqs.explain: Phantoms are new/removed rows appearing/disappearing in a repeated range query.

u:core-dbms-58-timestamp-ordering.title: Timestamp ordering
u:core-dbms-58-timestamp-ordering.summary: Order transactions by timestamp instead of locks, aborting those that violate the order.

blocks.text: **Timestamp ordering (TO)** is a lock-free concurrency-control protocol. Each transaction gets a unique **timestamp** at start; the schedule must be equivalent to running transactions in timestamp order.

items: Each data item tracks the max **read-timestamp** and **write-timestamp** of transactions that accessed it.
If a transaction tries an operation that would violate timestamp order (e.g. an older transaction writing an item a newer one already read), it's **aborted and restarted** with a new timestamp.
No locks, so **no deadlock** — but there can be **starvation** from repeated aborts (and cascading rollbacks unless made strict).

blocks.text: Timestamp ordering trades locking for aborts: it can't deadlock (no waiting), but transactions get aborted/restarted when they'd break the serial timestamp order. Contrast with 2PL, which waits (and can deadlock) rather than aborting.

mcqs.q: Timestamp ordering ensures serializability equivalent to running transactions in:
mcqs.explain: The protocol enforces a schedule equivalent to the serial order given by transaction timestamps.

mcqs.q: A key advantage of timestamp ordering over locking is:
mcqs.explain: Without locks/waiting, deadlock cannot occur — though repeated aborts can cause starvation.

mcqs.q: When an operation would violate timestamp order, the protocol:
options: Aborts and restarts the violating transaction
mcqs.explain: Rather than blocking, it rolls back the out-of-order transaction and restarts it with a new timestamp.

u:core-dbms-59-optimistic-concurrency.title: Optimistic concurrency
u:core-dbms-59-optimistic-concurrency.summary: Run without locking, then validate before commit — great when conflicts are rare.

blocks.text: **Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)** assumes conflicts are rare, so transactions run **without locks** and are only checked at the end. It has three phases:

items: **Read phase** — the transaction reads and makes changes to a private, local workspace.
**Validation phase** — before commit, it checks whether its reads/writes conflict with other transactions that committed meanwhile.
**Write phase** — if validation passes, changes are applied; otherwise the transaction is **aborted and restarted**.

blocks.text: OCC shines under **low contention**: no locking overhead on the happy path. Under **high contention** it degrades — many transactions fail validation and restart, wasting the work done. Locking (pessimistic) is better when conflicts are common.
OCC is common in web apps via a version column: read a row's version, and on update check the version hasn't changed (WHERE version = old_version), retrying if it has.

mcqs.q: Optimistic concurrency control performs conflict checking:
options: During a validation phase before commit
mcqs.explain: OCC runs lock-free and validates for conflicts only at commit time.

mcqs.q: OCC performs best when:
options: Locks are unavailable and contention is high
mcqs.explain: With few conflicts, most validations pass and the lock-free path is fast; high contention causes many restarts.

mcqs.q: If OCC validation fails, the transaction is:
mcqs.explain: A failed validation means a conflict occurred, so the transaction rolls back and retries.

u:core-dbms-60-deadlock-in-dbms-wait-die.title: Deadlock in DBMS: wait-die, wound-wait
u:core-dbms-60-deadlock-in-dbms-wait-die.summary: Timestamp-based deadlock-prevention schemes that decide whether to wait or abort.

blocks.text: Locking can deadlock. Beyond detection (wait-for graph) and timeouts, two **timestamp-based prevention** schemes decide, when a transaction needs a lock held by another, whether it waits or aborts — based on which is **older**.

Both use timestamps so a consistent age ordering prevents cycles: **Wait-Die** — old waits, young dies (non-preemptive); **Wound-Wait** — old preempts (wounds) young, young waits (preemptive). Older transactions are never aborted by younger ones in either scheme, avoiding starvation.
Mnemonic: in both, the older transaction is favoured. Wait-Die: only younger transactions die. Wound-Wait: only younger transactions get wounded.

mcqs.q: In the Wait-Die scheme, when an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one, it:
mcqs.explain: Wait-Die: an older requester waits; only a younger requester dies (aborts).

mcqs.q: Wound-Wait is a preemptive scheme where an older transaction:
options: Wounds (aborts) the younger lock holder and takes the lock
mcqs.explain: In Wound-Wait, the older transaction preempts (wounds) the younger holder; a younger requester waits.

mcqs.q: Both wait-die and wound-wait prevent deadlock by:
options: Enforcing a consistent age-based ordering so wait cycles can't form
mcqs.explain: A consistent ordering by timestamp (age) breaks the possibility of a circular wait.

u:core-dbms-31-aggregate-functions.title: Aggregate functions
u:core-dbms-31-aggregate-functions.summary: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — collapse many rows into one summary value.

blocks.text: **Aggregate functions** compute a single value over a set of rows: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`. They're used alone (whole table) or with `GROUP BY` (per group).

items: All aggregates **except COUNT(*)** ignore NULLs. `COUNT(col)` counts non-null values; `COUNT(*)` counts all rows.
`AVG(col)` = SUM(col)/COUNT(col), skipping NULLs — which can surprise you.
`COUNT(DISTINCT col)` counts unique non-null values.

blocks.text: The NULL behaviour is the tested point: aggregates skip NULLs, so AVG ignores missing values (not treating them as 0), and only COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs.

mcqs.q: Which counts every row, including those with NULLs in a column?
mcqs.explain: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) ignores NULLs in that column.

mcqs.q: AVG(col) computes the average over:
mcqs.explain: AVG ignores NULLs, dividing the sum of non-null values by their count — NULLs aren't treated as zero.

mcqs.q: To count unique non-null values you use:
mcqs.explain: COUNT(DISTINCT col) returns the number of distinct non-null values.

u:core-dbms-32-window-functions-row-numb.title: Window functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
u:core-dbms-32-window-functions-row-numb.summary: Compute per-row values over a related set of rows without collapsing them.

blocks.text: **Window functions** compute a value over a 'window' of rows related to the current row, but **without collapsing** them like GROUP BY does — every row is kept, with an extra computed column.

rows: Unique sequential number; ties get different numbers arbitrarily
Ties share a rank; the next rank SKIPS (1,1,3)
Ties share a rank; no gap (1,1,2)

blocks.text: The tie behaviour is the exam point: RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3), DENSE_RANK doesn't (1,1,2), and ROW_NUMBER always gives distinct numbers. `PARTITION BY` restarts the numbering per group.
Window functions are the clean way to solve 'top N per group' and 'Nth highest' — filter on the window's rank in an outer query.

mcqs.q: For salaries 100,100,90, RANK() assigns:
mcqs.explain: RANK gives ties the same rank and skips the next (1,1,3); DENSE_RANK would give 1,1,2.

mcqs.q: Unlike GROUP BY, a window function:
options: Keeps every row and adds a computed column over the window
mcqs.explain: Window functions don't collapse rows; they annotate each row with a value computed over its window.

mcqs.q: PARTITION BY in a window function:
options: Restarts the window computation for each group
mcqs.explain: It divides rows into partitions so the function computes independently within each.

u:core-dbms-33-partition-by-and-frames.title: PARTITION BY and frames
u:core-dbms-33-partition-by-and-frames.summary: Scope a window to groups and define the exact rows it spans for running calculations.

blocks.text: Two clauses shape a window function's window.

items: **PARTITION BY** — splits rows into groups; the function restarts per group (like GROUP BY, but rows are kept).

**Frame** (`ROWS BETWEEN ...`) — within an ordered partition, defines which rows the function sees relative to the current row: e.g. `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for a **running total**.

blocks.text: PARTITION BY sets the group; the frame sets the sliding range within it. Running totals, moving averages, and cumulative counts all come from choosing the right frame.

mcqs.q: A running total is produced by a window frame of:
mcqs.explain: Summing from the partition start up to the current row yields a cumulative/running total.

mcqs.q: PARTITION BY in a window definition:
options: Divides rows into groups the function computes over independently
mcqs.explain: It groups rows so each partition gets its own window computation.

mcqs.q: A moving average over the last 3 rows uses a frame like:
options: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
mcqs.explain: A sliding frame of the current row plus the two before it averages a 3-row window.

u:core-dbms-34-ctes-and-recursive-ctes.title: CTEs and recursive CTEs
u:core-dbms-34-ctes-and-recursive-ctes.summary: Named temporary result sets that make queries readable — and can recurse over hierarchies.

blocks.text: A **Common Table Expression (CTE)** is a named temporary result defined with `WITH`, usable in the main query. It improves readability and lets you reference the same subquery by name.
Recursive CTEs

A **recursive CTE** references itself, ideal for hierarchies (org charts, category trees, bill of materials). It has an **anchor** member (base rows) UNION ALL a **recursive** member that repeatedly joins back to the CTE until no new rows appear.
CTEs make complex queries readable by naming intermediate steps. Recursive CTEs are the standard SQL way to traverse arbitrary-depth hierarchies — something a single self join can't do.

mcqs.q: A CTE is defined using which keyword?
mcqs.explain: The WITH clause defines a named temporary result set (CTE).

mcqs.q: Recursive CTEs are especially useful for:
options: Traversing hierarchical/tree data of arbitrary depth
mcqs.explain: Their self-reference lets them walk parent-child hierarchies to any depth.

mcqs.q: A recursive CTE consists of:
options: An anchor member and a recursive member combined with UNION ALL
mcqs.explain: The anchor provides base rows; the recursive member repeatedly extends the result until it stops producing new rows.

u:core-dbms-35-views-and-materialised-vi.title: Views and materialised views
u:core-dbms-35-views-and-materialised-vi.summary: A saved query you use like a table — computed on the fly, or stored and refreshed.

blocks.text: A **view** is a named, stored query that behaves like a virtual table. Two kinds differ in whether results are stored.

items: Views simplify complex queries, provide a stable interface, and restrict access (a security layer showing only some columns/rows).
Materialised views trade freshness for speed — great for expensive aggregations refreshed periodically.

blocks.text: Plain view = query re-run each time (always fresh, no storage). Materialised view = stored snapshot (fast reads, must be refreshed, can be stale). Choose based on freshness vs read-cost.

mcqs.q: A regular (non-materialised) view stores:
options: Only the query definition; results are computed each time
A cached copy that never updates
mcqs.explain: A view is virtual — its query runs on access, so it always reflects current data.

mcqs.q: A materialised view improves read speed by:
options: Storing precomputed results (which can become stale until refreshed)
mcqs.explain: It caches the query output on disk, so reads are fast but data can be stale between refreshes.

mcqs.q: A common non-performance use of views is:
options: Providing a security layer that exposes only certain columns/rows
mcqs.explain: Views can restrict what users see, acting as an access-control abstraction.

u:core-dbms-36-stored-procedures-and-fun.title: Stored procedures and functions
u:core-dbms-36-stored-procedures-and-fun.summary: Precompiled routines stored in the database for reusable server-side logic.

blocks.text: A **stored procedure** is a named set of SQL statements stored in the DB and executed on demand. A **function** is similar but **returns a value** and can be used inside queries.

rows: Optional (via OUT params); may return none

blocks.text: Both encapsulate reusable server-side logic, reduce round-trips, and can improve security. The key difference: a function returns a value and is callable within a query; a procedure is invoked as a standalone command.
Heavy business logic in stored procedures can be hard to version-control and test; balance against keeping logic in the application.

mcqs.q: A key difference between a function and a stored procedure is that a function:
options: Returns a value and can be used inside a query
mcqs.explain: Functions return a value and are usable in SELECT/WHERE; procedures are invoked as commands.

mcqs.q: A benefit of stored procedures is:
options: Encapsulating reusable server-side logic and reducing round-trips
mcqs.explain: They run logic on the server in one call, cutting round-trips and centralising logic.

mcqs.q: Stored procedures and functions are:
options: Interpreted line by line each call with no reuse
Stored in the database and reusable
mcqs.explain: They live in the database as reusable, callable routines.

u:core-dbms-37-triggers.title: Triggers
u:core-dbms-37-triggers.summary: Procedural code that fires automatically in response to data-change events.

blocks.text: A **trigger** is code that runs **automatically** when a specified event (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) occurs on a table. It fires **BEFORE** or **AFTER** the event, for each row or per statement.

items: Uses: auditing (log every change), enforcing complex rules, maintaining derived data, cascading custom actions.
`BEFORE` triggers can modify the row being written; `AFTER` triggers react to the completed change.
Access to `OLD` and `NEW` row values.

blocks.text: Triggers run hidden 'magic' — they make behaviour implicit, can hurt performance, and can cause hard-to-debug cascades (one trigger firing another). Use sparingly and document them.
A trigger = event + timing (BEFORE/AFTER) + action. It's the tool for automatic auditing and enforcing rules that constraints can't express.

mcqs.q: A trigger executes:
options: Automatically in response to INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events
mcqs.explain: Triggers fire automatically on the data-modification events they're bound to.

mcqs.q: A common legitimate use of triggers is:
options: Auditing/logging every change to a table
mcqs.explain: Auditing changes automatically is a canonical trigger use case.

mcqs.q: A caution about triggers is that they:
options: Make behaviour implicit and can cause hard-to-debug cascades
mcqs.explain: Because they run automatically and can chain, triggers can be surprising and hard to trace.

u:core-dbms-38-nth-highest-salary-know-3.title: Nth highest salary (know 3 ways)
u:core-dbms-38-nth-highest-salary-know-3.summary: A staple SQL interview question with subquery, LIMIT/OFFSET, and window-function solutions.

blocks.text: Finding the Nth highest salary is a classic interview task. Know multiple approaches and their trade-offs.
1) Correlated subquery
2) LIMIT / OFFSET
3) Window function (cleanest)

Use DENSE_RANK for the Nth *distinct* salary (ties share a rank, no gaps). LIMIT/OFFSET is simplest but skips exactly N-1 rows (careful with duplicate salaries — add DISTINCT). The correlated subquery is portable but O(n^2).

mcqs.q: To get the Nth highest DISTINCT salary via a window function, use:
options: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = N
mcqs.explain: DENSE_RANK gives tied salaries the same rank with no gaps, so rank = N is the Nth distinct salary.

mcqs.q: The LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 approach requires care because:
options: Duplicate salaries can shift the offset; add DISTINCT to count distinct salaries
mcqs.explain: Without DISTINCT, duplicate salaries occupy separate rows, so the offset may not land on the Nth distinct value.

mcqs.q: The correlated-subquery approach's downside is:
options: It can be O(n^2), scanning per row
mcqs.explain: Counting greater salaries per row makes it quadratic on large tables, unlike the window-function version.

u:core-dbms-39-functional-dependencies.title: Functional dependencies
u:core-dbms-39-functional-dependencies.summary: X → Y means X's value determines Y's value — the basis of all normalization.

blocks.text: A **functional dependency (FD)** `X → Y` means: if two tuples agree on X, they must agree on Y. X **functionally determines** Y. FDs capture the real-world rules a schema must respect and drive normalization.

items: Example: `roll_no → name` (a roll number determines exactly one name).
**Trivial** FD: Y is a subset of X (always holds, e.g. {A,B} → A).
**Armstrong's axioms** (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) derive all implied FDs.

blocks.text: FDs are constraints on values, not on a particular table instance. X → Y is what lets us reason about keys and decide whether a table is well-designed (normalized) or needs decomposing.
A superkey is exactly a set of attributes that functionally determines every other attribute — FDs and keys are two sides of the same idea.

mcqs.q: The functional dependency X → Y means:
options: Any two tuples agreeing on X must agree on Y
mcqs.explain: X determines Y: equal X values force equal Y values.

mcqs.q: A trivial functional dependency is one where:
options: Y is a subset of X (it always holds)
mcqs.explain: If Y ⊆ X, then X → Y holds automatically — a trivial dependency.

mcqs.q: A superkey can be characterised by FDs as a set of attributes that:
options: Functionally determines all attributes of the relation
mcqs.explain: A superkey determines every attribute, which is the FD-based definition of a key.

u:core-dbms-40-attribute-closure.title: Attribute closure
u:core-dbms-40-attribute-closure.summary: Everything a set of attributes determines — the tool for finding keys.

blocks.text: The **closure** of an attribute set X (written **X+**) is the set of all attributes functionally determined by X, given the FDs. It's the workhorse for finding keys and testing FDs.
Algorithm

items: Start with X+ = X.
Repeat: if there's an FD A → B where A ⊆ X+, add B to X+.
Stop when X+ stops growing.

blocks.text: Two uses of closure: (1) X is a **superkey** iff X+ = all attributes; (2) an FD X → Y holds iff Y ⊆ X+. Computing closures is how you mechanically find candidate keys.
To find candidate keys: start from attributes that appear only on the LEFT of FDs (they must be in every key), compute their closure, and extend minimally until it covers all attributes.

mcqs.q: The attribute closure X+ is:
options: The set of all attributes functionally determined by X
mcqs.explain: X+ collects every attribute reachable from X via the FDs.

mcqs.q: X is a superkey if and only if:
options: X+ equals all attributes of the relation
mcqs.explain: If X determines every attribute (X+ = R), then X is a superkey.

mcqs.q: An FD X → Y holds (is implied by the given FDs) iff:
options: Y is a subset of X+
mcqs.explain: X → Y is derivable exactly when Y is in the closure of X.

u:core-dbms-41-finding-candidate-keys.title: Finding candidate keys
u:core-dbms-41-finding-candidate-keys.summary: Use closures and the left/right-side classification of attributes to enumerate minimal keys.

blocks.text: A **candidate key** is a minimal attribute set whose closure is all attributes. Finding them systematically avoids guesswork.

items: Classify attributes by where they appear in the FDs: **left-only** (must be in every key), **right-only** (never in a key), **both / neither**.
Attributes appearing ONLY on the left of FDs, plus any that appear in no FD, are in every candidate key — start with them.
Compute their closure. If it's already all attributes → that's the key.
Otherwise, add 'both-side' attributes one at a time (minimally) and recompute closure until it covers everything.

blocks.text: The shortcut: attributes that never appear on any right-hand side must be part of every key (nothing determines them). Start there, take the closure, and extend minimally.
A relation can have multiple candidate keys. 'Minimal' matters — a superkey with an extra attribute is not a candidate key.

mcqs.q: An attribute that appears only on the LEFT side of all FDs is:
options: Necessarily part of every candidate key
mcqs.explain: Nothing determines it, so it must be included in every key to reach it in a closure.

mcqs.q: A candidate key must be:
options: A minimal set of attributes whose closure is all attributes
mcqs.explain: Candidate keys are minimal superkeys — remove any attribute and closure no longer covers everything.

mcqs.q: An attribute appearing only on the RIGHT side of FDs is:
options: Not part of any candidate key
mcqs.explain: Right-only attributes are determined by others, so they need not (and can't minimally) be in a key.

u:core-dbms-42-1nf-2nf-3nf.title: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
u:core-dbms-42-1nf-2nf-3nf.summary: The first three normal forms: atomic values, no partial dependency, no transitive dependency.

blocks.text: **Normalization** removes redundancy and update anomalies by decomposing tables. The first three normal forms build on each other.

rows: All values atomic (no repeating groups/multivalued cells)
1NF + no partial dependency (non-key attr on PART of a composite key)

items: **2NF** only matters when the primary key is **composite** — a non-key attribute must depend on the whole key, not part of it.
**3NF**: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (e.g. `zip → city` in an employee table means city transitively depends on the key).

blocks.text: Memorable version (Codd): every non-key attribute must depend on 'the key (1NF/relation), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF), so help me Codd.'

mcqs.q: 1NF requires that:
options: All attribute values are atomic (no repeating groups)
mcqs.explain: First normal form demands atomic, single-valued columns — no lists or repeating groups.

mcqs.q: 2NF eliminates:
options: Partial dependency of a non-key attribute on part of a composite key
mcqs.explain: 2NF (relevant only with composite keys) removes dependencies on a subset of the key.

mcqs.q: 3NF removes:
options: Transitive dependencies (non-key attribute determined by another non-key attribute)
mcqs.explain: 3NF forbids a non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute.

u:core-dbms-43-bcnf.title: BCNF
u:core-dbms-43-bcnf.summary: A stricter 3NF: every determinant must be a superkey.

blocks.text: **Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)** is a stronger version of 3NF. A relation is in BCNF if for **every** non-trivial functional dependency `X → Y`, **X is a superkey**.

items: 3NF allows an exception (a non-key attribute can determine a prime attribute); BCNF removes it — the determinant must always be a superkey.
Most 3NF relations are already BCNF; the difference shows up with **overlapping candidate keys**.
BCNF decomposition is always **lossless** but may **not preserve all dependencies** — a real trade-off.

blocks.text: BCNF rule in one line: every determinant is a superkey. It's stricter than 3NF but decomposing to BCNF can lose dependency preservation, which is why 3NF is sometimes chosen instead.

mcqs.q: A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial FD X → Y:
mcqs.explain: BCNF requires the left side (determinant) of every non-trivial FD to be a superkey.

mcqs.q: BCNF is stricter than 3NF; the difference appears mainly with:
mcqs.explain: 3NF and BCNF differ when candidate keys overlap, allowing a 3NF relation that isn't BCNF.

mcqs.q: A trade-off of decomposing to BCNF is that it:
options: May not preserve all functional dependencies
mcqs.explain: BCNF decomposition is lossless but can fail to preserve every dependency, unlike 3NF which can always preserve them.

u:core-dbms-44-4nf-and-multivalued-depen.title: 4NF and multivalued dependencies
u:core-dbms-44-4nf-and-multivalued-depen.summary: Beyond BCNF: remove independent multivalued facts stored in one table.

blocks.text: A **multivalued dependency (MVD)** `X ->> Y` exists when, for each X, there's a set of Y values **independent** of the other attributes. Storing two independent multivalued facts together causes a combinatorial explosion of rows.
**4NF** requires BCNF plus no non-trivial multivalued dependencies (every MVD's determinant is a superkey). It's fixed by splitting the independent facts into separate tables.

Example: a `Student(name, hobby, language)` where hobbies and languages are independent forces a row per (hobby × language) combination — redundant. 4NF splits it into Student-Hobby and Student-Language.
Every FD is a special case of an MVD, and 4NF implies BCNF. If a table has one multivalued attribute it may be fine; the problem is two independent ones in the same table.

mcqs.q: 4NF deals with eliminating:
mcqs.explain: 4NF removes multivalued dependencies where independent multivalued facts are stored together.

mcqs.q: A multivalued dependency causes redundancy when a table stores:
options: Two independent multivalued facts together (their cross-product)
mcqs.explain: Two independent sets force a row per combination, exploding the row count redundantly.

mcqs.q: The fix for a 4NF violation is to:
options: Split the independent multivalued facts into separate tables
mcqs.explain: Decomposing the independent facts into their own relations removes the combinatorial redundancy.

u:core-dbms-45-lossless-join-decompositi.title: Lossless join decomposition
u:core-dbms-45-lossless-join-decompositi.summary: Split a table so that joining the pieces back reconstructs exactly the original — no spurious rows.

blocks.text: When we decompose a relation R into R1 and R2 for normalization, the decomposition must be **lossless**: rejoining R1 and R2 must give back **exactly** R — no lost rows and no extra (spurious) rows.
The test
A binary decomposition of R into R1, R2 is lossless if their **common attributes form a superkey of at least one** of them: `(R1 ∩ R2) → R1` **or** `(R1 ∩ R2) → R2`.

The shared column between the two tables must be a key of one of them. If it is, the join reconstructs R perfectly; if not, the join can generate spurious tuples — a lossy decomposition, which is unacceptable.
A lossy decomposition silently invents rows on rejoin, corrupting data. Every normalization decomposition must be checked for the lossless-join property.

mcqs.q: A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if the common attributes:
options: Form a superkey of R1 or of R2
mcqs.explain: If R1 ∩ R2 is a superkey of at least one piece, the natural join reconstructs R exactly.

mcqs.q: A lossy decomposition is problematic because rejoining the pieces:
options: Produces spurious (extra) tuples not in the original
mcqs.explain: Lossy joins fabricate rows that weren't in R, corrupting the data.

mcqs.q: Ensuring lossless join is required because normalization:
options: Splits tables and must be able to reconstruct the original exactly
mcqs.explain: Decomposition is only valid if the original relation can be recovered without loss or invention.

u:core-dbms-46-dependency-preservation.title: Dependency preservation
u:core-dbms-46-dependency-preservation.summary: Keep all functional dependencies checkable within individual tables after decomposition.

blocks.text: A decomposition is **dependency-preserving** if every original functional dependency can still be **enforced by checking a single decomposed table** — without having to join tables back together to validate a constraint.

items: If an FD spans two tables after decomposition, enforcing it needs a join on every update — expensive and awkward.
3NF decomposition can always be both **lossless AND dependency-preserving**.
BCNF decomposition is always lossless but **may sacrifice dependency preservation** — the key trade-off between 3NF and BCNF.

blocks.text: The 3NF vs BCNF decision comes down to this: 3NF guarantees lossless + dependency-preserving; BCNF guarantees lossless + fully non-redundant but might lose a dependency. Choose 3NF when preserving a dependency matters more than removing the last redundancy.

mcqs.q: A dependency-preserving decomposition allows every FD to be enforced by:
options: Checking a single decomposed table (no join needed)
mcqs.explain: Preservation means each FD lives within one table, so it can be validated without joins.

mcqs.q: Which normal form guarantees BOTH lossless join and dependency preservation?
mcqs.explain: A 3NF decomposition can always be made lossless and dependency-preserving; BCNF may lose dependency preservation.

mcqs.q: BCNF is sometimes avoided in favour of 3NF because BCNF:
options: May not preserve all functional dependencies
mcqs.explain: Achieving BCNF can require a decomposition that no longer preserves some dependency.

u:core-dbms-47-when-to-denormalise.title: When to denormalise
u:core-dbms-47-when-to-denormalise.summary: Deliberately reintroduce redundancy to speed reads — a conscious trade-off.

blocks.text: **Denormalisation** intentionally adds redundancy (duplicating data or precomputing joins/aggregates) to a normalized schema to **improve read performance**, accepting more complex writes.

items: Reasons: expensive joins on hot read paths, heavy aggregation, read-heavy workloads (analytics, dashboards).
Cost: update anomalies return — duplicated data must be kept in sync (via application logic, triggers, or scheduled jobs).
Common in data warehouses (star schemas) and caching layers.

blocks.text: Normalize first, denormalise deliberately for measured performance needs. Denormalisation trades write complexity and consistency risk for faster reads — only worth it when reads dominate and the join cost is proven.
Premature denormalisation is a classic mistake: it adds bugs and redundancy before any performance problem exists. Measure first.

mcqs.q: Denormalisation is primarily done to:
options: Improve read performance by adding redundancy/precomputed data
mcqs.explain: It trades extra redundancy for faster reads on read-heavy or join-heavy workloads.

mcqs.q: The main cost of denormalisation is:
options: Reintroduced update anomalies — duplicated data must be kept consistent
mcqs.explain: Duplicated/precomputed data can drift out of sync and must be maintained, complicating writes.

mcqs.q: A sound approach is to:
options: Normalize first and denormalise deliberately for measured performance needs
mcqs.explain: Denormalise only when a real, measured read-performance need justifies the added complexity.

u:core-dbms-16-ddl-create-alter-drop-tru.title: DDL: create, alter, drop, truncate
u:core-dbms-16-ddl-create-alter-drop-tru.summary: Data Definition Language commands that shape the schema — and how DROP, DELETE, and TRUNCATE differ.

blocks.text: **DDL (Data Definition Language)** defines and modifies database structure: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`. DDL statements are auto-committed (they can't easily be rolled back).

rows: Remove all rows but keep the table structure

blocks.text: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
The classic trap: DELETE is DML (row-by-row, WHERE-able, rollback-able); TRUNCATE is DDL (all rows, fast, resets, not easily rolled back); DROP removes the table itself.

mcqs.q: Which removes all rows but keeps the table structure and is typically not rolled back?
mcqs.explain: TRUNCATE (DDL) quickly removes all rows and keeps the structure, but usually can't be rolled back like DELETE.

mcqs.q: DELETE differs from TRUNCATE because DELETE:
options: Can filter rows with WHERE and is transactional (rollback-able)
mcqs.explain: DELETE is DML: it supports WHERE and participates in transactions, unlike TRUNCATE.

mcqs.q: DROP TABLE removes:
options: The entire table including its structure
mcqs.explain: DROP deletes the whole table object — data and schema.

u:core-dbms-17-dml-insert-update-delete.title: DML: insert, update, delete
u:core-dbms-17-dml-insert-update-delete.summary: The commands that change table data, all transactional.

blocks.text: **DML (Data Manipulation Language)** changes the data inside tables: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` (and `SELECT` for reading). DML runs within transactions, so changes can be committed or rolled back.
Always use a WHERE clause with UPDATE and DELETE. `UPDATE users SET name='x';` without WHERE changes every row — a common and costly mistake.
DML is transactional: until you COMMIT, changes can be rolled back. This is what makes multi-step data changes safe.

mcqs.q: Which set of commands is DML?
mcqs.explain: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (and SELECT) manipulate data — DML; CREATE/DROP/ALTER are DDL.

mcqs.q: Running `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0;` with no WHERE clause:
options: Updates every row in the table
mcqs.explain: Without WHERE, UPDATE affects all rows — a dangerous omission.

mcqs.q: DML changes can be undone before commit because DML is:
mcqs.explain: DML runs inside transactions, so ROLLBACK can undo uncommitted changes.

u:core-dbms-18-constraints-not-null-uniq.title: Constraints: not null, unique, check, default
u:core-dbms-18-constraints-not-null-uniq.summary: Column-level rules the database enforces automatically on every write.

blocks.text: **Constraints** are rules enforced by the DBMS to keep data valid, checked on every insert/update.

rows: No duplicate values (allows one NULL, usually)
UNIQUE + NOT NULL, the row identifier
Value must exist in the referenced table
Value used when none is supplied

blocks.text: Constraints push data-validity rules into the database itself, so no application bug can insert invalid data. UNIQUE differs from PRIMARY KEY by allowing a NULL and permitting multiple unique columns per table.

mcqs.q: The difference between UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY is that UNIQUE:
options: Allows a NULL and a table can have several UNIQUE columns
mcqs.explain: A primary key is UNIQUE + NOT NULL and only one per table; UNIQUE permits a NULL and multiple columns.

mcqs.q: A rule like 'salary >= 0' is enforced with a:
mcqs.explain: CHECK enforces an arbitrary boolean condition on a column's values.

mcqs.q: A DEFAULT constraint provides:
options: A value used when the insert omits that column
mcqs.explain: DEFAULT supplies a value automatically when none is given during insert.

u:core-dbms-19-select-where-order-by-lim.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
u:core-dbms-19-select-where-order-by-lim.summary: The core read query — filter rows, sort them, and cap the count.

blocks.text: The `SELECT` statement retrieves rows. Its clauses run in a logical order that isn't the written order.

SELECT name, marks
FROM students
WHERE marks >= 40
ORDER BY marks DESC
LIMIT 10;
Logical execution order
**FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT**. This is why you can't reference a SELECT alias in WHERE (WHERE runs before SELECT) but can in ORDER BY.
Written order (SELECT first) is not execution order (FROM/WHERE first). Understanding that WHERE runs before SELECT explains many 'unknown column' alias errors.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. LIMIT/OFFSET is used for pagination.

mcqs.q: What is the logical execution order of these clauses?
mcqs.explain: FROM and WHERE run before SELECT and ORDER BY, which is why SELECT aliases aren't visible in WHERE.

mcqs.q: You cannot use a SELECT-list alias in the WHERE clause because:
options: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT computes the alias
mcqs.explain: Since WHERE executes before SELECT, the alias doesn't exist yet at WHERE time.

mcqs.q: ORDER BY DESC sorts results:
