mcqs.explain: DESC orders from highest to lowest; ASC (default) is lowest to highest.

u:core-dbms-20-group-by-and-having.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
u:core-dbms-20-group-by-and-having.summary: Collapse rows into groups for aggregation, then filter the groups with HAVING.

blocks.text: `GROUP BY` collapses rows sharing a value into a single group so aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG…) compute per group. `HAVING` then filters those groups.

SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

items: **WHERE** filters rows **before** grouping; **HAVING** filters groups **after** aggregation.
Any non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY.
You can't use an aggregate in WHERE — that's what HAVING is for.

blocks.text: The distinction: WHERE (before grouping, per-row) vs HAVING (after grouping, per-group). 'HAVING COUNT(*) > 5' can't be done in WHERE because the count doesn't exist until groups form.

mcqs.q: HAVING differs from WHERE because HAVING:
mcqs.explain: WHERE filters pre-grouping rows; HAVING filters the aggregated groups.

mcqs.q: To find departments with more than 5 employees you use:
mcqs.explain: Aggregates like COUNT can only be filtered with HAVING after GROUP BY, not in WHERE.

mcqs.q: A non-aggregated column in the SELECT list of a grouped query must:
options: Appear in the GROUP BY clause
mcqs.explain: Every selected non-aggregate column must be part of GROUP BY (in standard SQL).

u:core-dbms-21-distinct-and-aliases.title: DISTINCT and aliases
u:core-dbms-21-distinct-and-aliases.summary: Remove duplicate rows and give columns/tables readable temporary names.

blocks.text: **DISTINCT** removes duplicate rows from a result set. **Aliases** (`AS`) rename a column or table for readability or to reference derived values.

items: `DISTINCT` applies to the whole selected row (the combination of columns), not one column.
Table aliases (`orders o`) shorten queries and are required for self-joins.
Column aliases can be referenced in ORDER BY (but not WHERE).

blocks.text: DISTINCT can be expensive (it sorts/hashes to dedupe). If duplicates come from a join fan-out, fixing the join is better than masking it with DISTINCT.

mcqs.q: SELECT DISTINCT applied to multiple columns removes duplicates based on:
options: The whole combination of selected columns
mcqs.explain: DISTINCT dedupes on the entire selected row, i.e. the combination of all listed columns.

mcqs.q: A table alias is required when:
options: Performing a self-join (joining a table to itself)
mcqs.explain: Self-joins need two aliases to distinguish the two references to the same table.

mcqs.q: A column alias defined in SELECT can be referenced in:
mcqs.explain: Because ORDER BY runs after SELECT, it can use the alias; WHERE (running earlier) cannot.

u:core-dbms-22-null-semantics-and-three-.title: NULL semantics and three-valued logic
u:core-dbms-22-null-semantics-and-three-.summary: NULL means 'unknown', so comparisons with it yield UNKNOWN, not true/false.

blocks.text: **NULL** represents a missing or unknown value — not zero, not empty string. This introduces **three-valued logic**: TRUE, FALSE, and **UNKNOWN**.

items: Any comparison with NULL yields **UNKNOWN**: `x = NULL` is never TRUE (even `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN). Use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.
WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is **TRUE** — so UNKNOWN rows are excluded.
Aggregates (except COUNT(*)) **ignore** NULLs. COUNT(col) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts all rows.
NULLs affect uniqueness and joins (they don't match each other).

blocks.text: The rule to remember: comparisons with NULL are UNKNOWN, and WHERE requires TRUE. That's why `WHERE col = NULL` returns nothing and you must write `col IS NULL`.
`NOT IN (subquery)` breaks if the subquery returns any NULL — the whole predicate becomes UNKNOWN and no rows match. Prefer NOT EXISTS in that case.

mcqs.q: The expression `salary = NULL` evaluates to:
mcqs.explain: Comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN; you must use IS NULL to test for null.

mcqs.q: Which counts rows including those with NULL in the column?
mcqs.explain: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) and other aggregates ignore NULLs.

mcqs.q: A WHERE clause returns a row only when its condition is:
mcqs.explain: Only TRUE rows are kept; UNKNOWN (from NULL comparisons) rows are excluded.

u:core-dbms-23-inner-join.title: Inner join
u:core-dbms-23-inner-join.summary: Return only rows that have a match on both sides of the join condition.

blocks.text: An **INNER JOIN** combines rows from two tables where the join condition matches, returning **only** the rows that have a counterpart in both tables. Unmatched rows are dropped.

items: Rows in either table with no match are excluded.
The join condition is usually FK = PK equality.
It's the most common join and the default when you write just `JOIN`.

blocks.text: Inner join = intersection of matches. If you need unmatched rows too (customers with no orders), you need an OUTER join instead.

mcqs.q: An INNER JOIN returns:
options: Only rows with a match in both tables
All rows from the left table
mcqs.explain: Inner join keeps only rows that satisfy the join condition on both sides.

mcqs.q: A customer with no orders will appear in an INNER JOIN of customers and orders:
mcqs.explain: With no matching order, the customer is dropped by the inner join (an outer join would keep it).

mcqs.q: Writing just `JOIN` in SQL defaults to:
mcqs.explain: The bare keyword JOIN means INNER JOIN.

u:core-dbms-24-left-right-full-outer-joi.title: Left, right, full outer join
u:core-dbms-24-left-right-full-outer-joi.summary: Keep unmatched rows from one or both sides, filling missing columns with NULL.

blocks.text: **Outer joins** keep unmatched rows and pad the missing side with NULLs.

rows: All left rows + matches from the right (NULLs where no match)
All right rows + matches from the left
All rows from both sides, matched where possible

blocks.text: Use LEFT JOIN to answer 'all customers, with their orders if any' — customers with no orders still appear with NULL order columns. Filtering `WHERE right.id IS NULL` after a LEFT JOIN finds rows with NO match (an anti-join).
A RIGHT JOIN is just a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped; most people standardise on LEFT for readability.

mcqs.q: A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns:
options: All rows from the left table, with NULLs where the right has no match
All rows from the right table
mcqs.explain: Left join keeps every left-table row and fills right-side columns with NULL when there's no match.

mcqs.q: To find customers with NO orders, you can use a LEFT JOIN and then:
mcqs.explain: Unmatched customers have NULL order columns; filtering IS NULL isolates them (anti-join).

mcqs.q: A FULL OUTER JOIN returns:
options: All rows from both tables, matched where possible
mcqs.explain: Full outer join keeps unmatched rows from both sides, padding with NULLs.

u:core-dbms-25-self-join.title: Self join
u:core-dbms-25-self-join.summary: Join a table to itself, using aliases, to relate rows within the same table.

blocks.text: A **self join** joins a table to itself, treating it as two copies via **aliases**. It relates rows within the same table — e.g. employees to their managers, where both are in one `employees` table.
The self join needs two aliases (e, m) so the query can reference the same table as two logical roles. It's the standard way to handle hierarchical/recursive-ish relationships stored in one table.
For deep hierarchies (all ancestors), a self join only goes one level — use a recursive CTE for arbitrary depth.

mcqs.q: A self join is used to:
options: Relate rows within the same table by joining it to itself
mcqs.explain: It joins a table to itself (via aliases) to relate its own rows, like employee↔manager.

mcqs.q: A self join requires:
options: Table aliases to distinguish the two copies
mcqs.explain: Aliases give the two logical roles of the same table distinct names.

mcqs.q: To find ALL ancestors up a hierarchy (arbitrary depth), better than a single self join is:
mcqs.explain: A single self join reaches one level; a recursive CTE walks the hierarchy to any depth.

u:core-dbms-26-cross-join.title: Cross join
u:core-dbms-26-cross-join.summary: The Cartesian product — every row of A paired with every row of B.

blocks.text: A **CROSS JOIN** produces the **Cartesian product**: every row of the first table combined with every row of the second. If A has m rows and B has n rows, the result has **m × n** rows and no join condition.

SELECT s.name, c.title
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colours c;   -- all size/colour combinations
An accidental cross join is a common bug: forgetting the ON condition (or a missing join key) makes a normal join explode into m×n rows — often the cause of a query returning far too many rows.
Legitimate uses: generating all combinations (sizes × colours), or pairing every row with a single-row table of constants.

mcqs.q: A CROSS JOIN of tables with m and n rows returns:
mcqs.explain: The Cartesian product pairs every row of one with every row of the other: m × n rows.

mcqs.q: A CROSS JOIN has:
mcqs.explain: Cross join combines all rows unconditionally — there is no ON clause.

mcqs.q: Forgetting the join condition in an inner join often produces:
options: An accidental Cartesian product (too many rows)
mcqs.explain: Without a join predicate the join degenerates into a cross join, exploding the row count.

u:core-dbms-27-natural-join-vs-explicit-.title: Natural join vs explicit ON
u:core-dbms-27-natural-join-vs-explicit-.summary: Auto-matching same-named columns vs stating the join condition explicitly.

blocks.text: A **NATURAL JOIN** automatically joins on **all columns with the same name** in both tables and merges those columns. An **explicit `JOIN ... ON`** states the condition yourself.

Natural join is dangerous: it silently joins on every same-named column, so an accidental shared column name (like `created_at` or `id`) changes results unexpectedly, and schema changes can break it. Prefer explicit ON.
Explicit `ON` is clearer and safer — you control exactly which columns join. Natural join's convenience isn't worth its fragility in real schemas.

mcqs.q: A NATURAL JOIN joins on:
options: All columns having the same name in both tables
mcqs.explain: It automatically matches every identically-named column, which can be surprising.

mcqs.q: Why is explicit JOIN ... ON generally preferred over NATURAL JOIN?
options: It makes the join condition explicit and avoids accidental matches on same-named columns
mcqs.explain: Explicit ON is clear and robust to schema changes, unlike natural join's implicit matching.

mcqs.q: Adding a new same-named column to both tables can break a NATURAL JOIN because:
options: The join now also matches on that new column, changing results
It converts to a cross join
mcqs.explain: Natural join includes every shared column name, so new shared names silently alter the join.

u:core-dbms-28-subqueries-and-correlated.title: Subqueries and correlated subqueries
u:core-dbms-28-subqueries-and-correlated.summary: A query inside a query — and the correlated kind that re-runs per outer row.

blocks.text: A **subquery** is a query nested inside another. A **non-correlated** subquery is independent (runs once). A **correlated** subquery references the outer query and is (conceptually) evaluated **once per outer row**.

items: Subqueries appear in WHERE, FROM (derived tables), or SELECT.
Non-correlated: evaluated once, result reused.
Correlated: depends on the current outer row, so re-evaluated per row — potentially slow.

blocks.text: The distinction: a correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it can't run standalone and logically runs per outer row. Non-correlated subqueries run once. Correlated ones can often be rewritten as joins for speed.

mcqs.q: A correlated subquery is one that:
options: References a column from the outer query, evaluated per outer row
mcqs.explain: It depends on the outer row's values, so conceptually it re-runs for each outer row.

mcqs.q: A non-correlated subquery is executed:
options: Once, independently, with its result reused
mcqs.explain: Being independent of the outer query, it evaluates a single time.

mcqs.q: Correlated subqueries can often be optimised by rewriting them as:
mcqs.explain: Turning a per-row subquery into a set-based join often improves performance.

u:core-dbms-29-exists-vs-in-vs-any-all.title: EXISTS vs IN vs ANY/ALL
u:core-dbms-29-exists-vs-in-vs-any-all.summary: Membership and quantified comparison operators — and the NULL trap with NOT IN.

blocks.text: These operators test a value against a subquery's results.

items: **IN** — true if the value equals any value in the list/subquery.
**EXISTS** — true if the subquery returns **any** row (checks existence, not values); often correlated.
**ANY / SOME** — comparison true for at least one (`> ANY` = greater than the minimum).
**ALL** — comparison true for all (`> ALL` = greater than the maximum).

blocks.text: The classic bug: `NOT IN (subquery)` returns no rows if the subquery contains any NULL, because the comparison becomes UNKNOWN. Use **NOT EXISTS** instead, which is NULL-safe.
EXISTS can short-circuit (stops at the first matching row) and pairs naturally with correlated subqueries; IN materialises the list.

mcqs.q: `NOT IN` with a subquery that returns a NULL will:
options: Return no rows because the comparison becomes UNKNOWN
mcqs.explain: A NULL in the NOT IN list makes the predicate UNKNOWN for all rows, returning nothing; NOT EXISTS avoids this.

mcqs.q: EXISTS returns TRUE when the subquery:
mcqs.explain: EXISTS checks for the presence of any row, regardless of its values.

mcqs.q: `x > ALL (subquery)` is true when x is greater than:
options: The maximum value in the subquery
mcqs.explain: > ALL requires x to exceed every value, i.e. the maximum; > ANY needs only to exceed the minimum.

u:core-dbms-30-union-vs-union-all-vs-int.title: UNION vs UNION ALL vs INTERSECT vs EXCEPT
u:core-dbms-30-union-vs-union-all-vs-int.summary: Set operators combining query results — and why UNION ALL is faster.

blocks.text: Set operators combine the results of two SELECTs that are **union-compatible** (same number of columns, compatible types).

rows: All rows from both, duplicates REMOVED
All rows from both, duplicates KEPT (faster)
Rows in the first but not the second

blocks.text: UNION removes duplicates (a costly sort/hash); UNION ALL keeps them and is faster. Use UNION ALL when you know there are no duplicates or don't care — it avoids the dedup work.
Set operators require the two SELECTs to have the same number of columns with compatible types, matched by position (not name).

mcqs.q: UNION differs from UNION ALL because UNION:
mcqs.explain: UNION dedupes the combined result; UNION ALL keeps duplicates and skips that work, so it's faster.

mcqs.q: INTERSECT returns rows that:
mcqs.explain: INTERSECT is the set intersection — rows common to both result sets.

mcqs.q: EXCEPT (MINUS) returns rows in:
options: The first query but not the second
mcqs.explain: EXCEPT is set difference: rows of the first query not present in the second.

u:core-dbms-0-dbms-vs-file-system.title: DBMS vs file system
u:core-dbms-0-dbms-vs-file-system.summary: Why databases replaced flat files: no redundancy, enforced integrity, concurrency, and querying.

blocks.text: A **DBMS** is software that manages structured data with querying, integrity, concurrency, and recovery — solving the problems of storing data in plain files.

The DBMS advantage in one line: it centralises data with guarantees — no redundancy, enforced integrity, safe concurrent access, crash recovery, and a query language — that ad-hoc file handling can't provide.

mcqs.q: Which is a core advantage of a DBMS over a flat-file system?
options: Controlled redundancy, enforced integrity, and concurrent access
mcqs.explain: A DBMS reduces redundancy, enforces constraints, and safely handles concurrent access — things flat files don't.

mcqs.q: Concurrent access without corruption is achieved in a DBMS via:
mcqs.explain: Transactions with concurrency control let many users modify data safely.

mcqs.q: Enforcing that an order must reference a valid customer is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Foreign-key/referential integrity constraints keep related data valid — a DBMS feature files lack.

u:core-dbms-1-three-level-architecture.title: Three-level architecture
u:core-dbms-1-three-level-architecture.summary: External, conceptual, and internal schemas — the ANSI-SPARC separation that enables data independence.

blocks.text: The **ANSI-SPARC three-level architecture** separates a database into three schema levels so users are insulated from storage details.

rows: The whole DB's logical structure (tables, relationships, constraints)
How data is physically stored (files, indexes)

blocks.text: Separating these levels is what gives **data independence**: you can change storage (internal) without touching the logical design, and change the logical design without breaking each user's view. The mappings between levels absorb the change.
External = views tailored per user; Conceptual = the one true schema; Internal = bytes on disk. Two mappings connect them (external↔conceptual, conceptual↔internal).

mcqs.q: The conceptual level of the three-level architecture describes:
options: The overall logical structure of the whole database
mcqs.explain: The conceptual (logical) schema is the community view of the entire database structure and constraints.

mcqs.q: The three-level architecture's main benefit is:
options: Data independence — changing one level without disrupting others
mcqs.explain: Insulating levels via mappings lets storage or logical changes happen without breaking user views.

mcqs.q: A per-user customised view of the data lives at the:
mcqs.explain: The external (view) level presents tailored subsets of the data to different users/applications.

u:core-dbms-2-logical-and-physical-data-.title: Logical and physical data independence
u:core-dbms-2-logical-and-physical-data-.summary: Change the schema or the storage without rewriting the layers above.

blocks.text: **Data independence** is the ability to change a schema at one level without altering the level above it — the payoff of the three-level architecture.

items: **Physical data independence** — change how data is stored (add an index, reorganise files, switch storage engine) without changing the conceptual/logical schema. This is easier to achieve and common.
**Logical data independence** — change the logical schema (add a column, split a table) without changing external views/applications. This is harder because views depend on the logical structure.

blocks.text: Physical independence (storage vs logical) is easily achieved; logical independence (logical vs external views) is harder because applications are tied more directly to the logical schema.

mcqs.q: Adding an index to speed up queries without changing the logical schema is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Changing physical storage (indexes) without affecting the conceptual schema is physical data independence.

mcqs.q: Which type of data independence is generally harder to achieve?
mcqs.explain: Logical independence is harder because external views and applications depend closely on the logical schema.

mcqs.q: Logical data independence means changing the logical schema without affecting:
mcqs.explain: It insulates user-level external schemas/applications from logical-schema changes.

u:core-dbms-3-dba-roles.title: DBA roles
u:core-dbms-3-dba-roles.summary: The database administrator owns schema, security, performance, and recovery.

blocks.text: The **Database Administrator (DBA)** is responsible for the database's design, health, and safety.

items: **Schema definition** — designing tables, relationships, constraints.
**Access control & security** — creating users/roles, granting/revoking privileges.
**Performance tuning** — indexes, query optimisation, storage layout.
**Backup & recovery** — ensuring data can be restored after failure.
**Integrity & maintenance** — constraints, upgrades, monitoring.

blocks.text: Think of the DBA as owning the four pillars: structure (schema), security (access), speed (tuning), and safety (backup/recovery).

mcqs.q: Granting and revoking user privileges is a DBA responsibility under:
mcqs.explain: Managing users, roles, and privileges is the DBA's security/access-control duty.

mcqs.q: Ensuring the database can be restored after a crash falls under:
mcqs.explain: Backup and recovery planning is a key DBA responsibility for data safety.

mcqs.q: Deciding which columns to index to speed queries is part of:
mcqs.explain: Index and query tuning is the DBA's performance responsibility.

u:core-dbms-4-data-models-overview.title: Data models overview
u:core-dbms-4-data-models-overview.summary: Relational, hierarchical, network, object, and NoSQL models — how data is structured.

blocks.text: A **data model** defines how data is logically structured and related. The dominant one is relational, but several exist.

rows: Tables (relations) of rows and columns; links via keys
Tree — each child has one parent (IBM IMS)
Graph — children can have multiple parents
Flexible schemas for scale and specific access patterns

blocks.text: The relational model won because of its simplicity (just tables), strong theory (relational algebra), and declarative querying (SQL). NoSQL models trade some of that for scale and schema flexibility.

mcqs.q: The relational model organises data as:
mcqs.explain: Relational databases store data in tables with rows (tuples) and columns (attributes).

mcqs.q: In the hierarchical model, each child record has:
mcqs.explain: Hierarchical models form a tree where each child links to a single parent.

mcqs.q: A reason the relational model became dominant is:
options: Simplicity plus a strong theoretical basis and declarative SQL
mcqs.explain: Simple tables, relational algebra, and SQL made it powerful and accessible.

u:core-dbms-5-entities-attributes-relati.title: Entities, attributes, relationships
u:core-dbms-5-entities-attributes-relati.summary: The vocabulary of ER modelling: things, their properties, and how they connect.

blocks.text: **ER (Entity-Relationship) modelling** describes data before it becomes tables.

items: **Entity** — a real-world object/thing (Student, Course). An **entity set** is a collection of them.
**Attribute** — a property of an entity (name, roll_no). Types: simple vs composite, single vs **multivalued**, stored vs **derived**, and the **key attribute** that uniquely identifies.
**Relationship** — an association between entities (a Student *enrols in* a Course). Relationships can have their own attributes (e.g. enrolment date).

blocks.text: Entities become tables, attributes become columns, and relationships become foreign keys or link tables. Getting the ER model right is the foundation of a clean schema.
Attribute types to recognise: composite (address → street, city), multivalued (phone numbers), derived (age from DOB), and the key attribute (usually underlined in an ER diagram).

mcqs.q: In ER modelling, a real-world object such as 'Student' is a(n):
mcqs.explain: An entity represents a distinguishable real-world thing; a collection of them is an entity set.

mcqs.q: 'Age' computed from date of birth is which kind of attribute?
mcqs.explain: A derived attribute is calculated from other stored data rather than stored directly.

mcqs.q: An 'enrolment date' stored on the enrols-in association is:
mcqs.explain: Relationships can carry their own attributes, such as when the association occurred.

u:core-dbms-6-weak-entities.title: Weak entities
u:core-dbms-6-weak-entities.summary: An entity that can't be identified on its own — it depends on an owner entity for identity.

blocks.text: A **weak entity** has no key attribute of its own; it can only be uniquely identified in combination with an **owner (strong) entity** via an **identifying relationship**.

items: It has a **partial key** (discriminator) that is unique only within one owner.
Its full identity = owner's key + its partial key.
Example: a `Dependent` (of an employee) — two employees can both have a dependent named 'Alex'; the dependent is identified only together with its employee.

blocks.text: Weak entity = existence-dependent + no key of its own. When mapped to a table, its primary key includes the owner's primary key as a foreign key plus its partial key.
In ER diagrams, weak entities and their identifying relationships are drawn with double rectangles/diamonds; the partial key is dashed-underlined.

mcqs.q: A weak entity is one that:
options: Has a primary key of its own
Cannot be uniquely identified without an owner entity
mcqs.explain: A weak entity lacks its own key and depends on an owner (strong) entity for identification.

mcqs.q: The primary key of a weak entity's table typically consists of:
options: The owner's primary key plus its own partial key (discriminator)
mcqs.explain: Its full identity combines the owner's key (as a foreign key) with its partial discriminator.

mcqs.q: The relationship connecting a weak entity to its owner is called:
mcqs.explain: The identifying relationship links the weak entity to the owner that provides its identity.

u:core-dbms-7-cardinality-and-participat.title: Cardinality and participation
u:core-dbms-7-cardinality-and-participat.summary: How many entities relate (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and whether every entity must participate.

blocks.text: Two constraints describe a relationship's shape.

items: **Cardinality ratio** — how many instances relate: **1:1**, **1:N** (one-to-many), or **M:N** (many-to-many).
**Participation** — **total** (every entity must participate, drawn as a double line) or **partial** (participation optional).

rows: FK on either side (often with unique)

blocks.text: Cardinality decides how the relationship becomes foreign keys: 1:N puts the FK on the many side, while M:N always needs a separate junction table holding both keys. Total participation often becomes a NOT NULL foreign key.

mcqs.q: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship is mapped to tables using:
options: A foreign key on one side
A separate junction (link) table with both keys
mcqs.explain: M:N can't be represented by a single FK; a junction table holding both primary keys resolves it.

mcqs.q: Total participation of an entity in a relationship means:
options: The entity may or may not participate
Every instance of that entity must participate
mcqs.explain: Total participation requires every entity instance to be involved in the relationship (double line in ER).

mcqs.q: In a 1:N relationship, the foreign key is placed on:
mcqs.explain: The many side stores the foreign key referencing the one side (e.g. each employee stores its department).

u:core-dbms-8-generalisation-specialisat.title: Generalisation, specialisation, aggregation
u:core-dbms-8-generalisation-specialisat.summary: The EER extensions: bottom-up grouping, top-down splitting, and treating a relationship as an entity.

blocks.text: Enhanced ER (EER) adds abstraction mechanisms similar to OOP inheritance.

items: **Generalisation** (bottom-up) — combine similar entities into a general superclass. Car and Truck → Vehicle.
**Specialisation** (top-down) — split an entity into subclasses with distinct attributes. Employee → Manager, Engineer.
**Aggregation** — treat a whole relationship (with its entities) as a single higher-level entity so another relationship can connect to it.

blocks.text: Generalisation and specialisation are two directions of the same is-a hierarchy (merge up vs split down). Aggregation is different: it lets a relationship participate in another relationship by abstracting it as an entity.
Aggregation example: a `works-on(Employee, Project)` relationship, aggregated, can then relate to a `Manager` who manages that whole works-on association.

mcqs.q: Combining Car and Truck into a common Vehicle superclass is:
mcqs.explain: Generalisation groups similar entities upward into a general superclass.

mcqs.q: Aggregation in EER is used to:
options: Treat a relationship (with its entities) as a higher-level entity so another relationship can link to it
mcqs.explain: Aggregation abstracts a relationship as an entity so it can participate in further relationships.

mcqs.q: Specialisation is:
options: Top-down splitting of an entity into subclasses with distinct attributes
mcqs.explain: Specialisation refines a superclass into subclasses (e.g. Employee → Manager/Engineer).

u:core-dbms-9-er-to-relational-mapping.title: ER to relational mapping
u:core-dbms-9-er-to-relational-mapping.summary: Systematic rules to turn an ER diagram into tables.

blocks.text: Converting an ER model to relational tables follows fixed rules.

items: **Strong entity** → a table; its key attribute → primary key.
**Weak entity** → a table whose PK = owner's PK (as FK) + partial key.
**1:1** → put a foreign key on either side (usually the total-participation side).
**1:N** → put the foreign key on the **many** side.
**M:N** → create a **junction table** with both entities' primary keys as a composite key.
**Multivalued attribute** → its own table (entity key + the value).
**Composite attribute** → store the component parts as separate columns.

blocks.text: The two rules that matter most: 1:N → FK on the many side; M:N → a separate junction table. Multivalued attributes also become their own table.

mcqs.q: A multivalued attribute (e.g. multiple phone numbers) is mapped to:
options: A separate table keyed by the entity's PK plus the value
mcqs.explain: Multivalued attributes need their own table so each value is a separate row.

mcqs.q: An M:N relationship becomes:
options: A foreign key on one side
A junction table with both entities' primary keys
mcqs.explain: Mapping M:N requires a link table holding the two primary keys as a composite key.

mcqs.q: A weak entity's table primary key is:
options: The owner's primary key plus the partial key
mcqs.explain: The weak entity is identified by combining the owner's key with its own discriminator.

u:core-dbms-10-relations-tuples-domains.title: Relations, tuples, domains
u:core-dbms-10-relations-tuples-domains.summary: The precise vocabulary of the relational model: table, row, and the allowed set of values.

blocks.text: The relational model has exact terms behind the casual 'table/row/column'.

rows: The set of allowed values for an attribute

items: A relation is a **set** of tuples — so (formally) no duplicate rows and no inherent order.
A **domain** constrains an attribute's values (e.g. age is a positive integer).

blocks.text: Because a relation is a set, it has no duplicate tuples and no ordering by definition. (Real SQL tables allow duplicates unless a key/constraint prevents them — a practical deviation from the pure model.)

mcqs.q: In the relational model, a 'tuple' corresponds to a:
mcqs.explain: A tuple is a row of a relation; an attribute is a column.

mcqs.q: The 'domain' of an attribute is:
options: The set of permissible values for that attribute
mcqs.explain: A domain defines the allowed values (type/range) an attribute can take.

mcqs.q: The 'degree' of a relation is the number of:
mcqs.explain: Degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.

u:core-dbms-11-super-key-candidate-key-p.title: Super key, candidate key, primary key, alternate key
u:core-dbms-11-super-key-candidate-key-p.summary: The hierarchy of keys — from any unique set down to the chosen identifier.

blocks.text: Keys uniquely identify tuples; they form a hierarchy from broad to specific.

items: **Super key** — any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple (may have extra, redundant attributes).
**Candidate key** — a **minimal** super key (no attribute can be removed while keeping uniqueness). A relation can have several.
**Primary key** — the candidate key chosen as the main identifier; it cannot be NULL.
**Alternate key** — a candidate key not chosen as primary.
**Composite key** — a key made of more than one attribute.

blocks.text: Chain of specificity: super key ⊇ candidate key (minimal super key) → one becomes the primary key, the rest are alternate keys. 'Minimal' is the word that separates candidate from super key.
Example: {roll_no}, {email} may each be candidate keys; pick {roll_no} as primary → {email} is an alternate key. {roll_no, name} is a super key but not candidate (name is redundant).

mcqs.q: A candidate key differs from a super key in that a candidate key is:
options: Minimal — no attribute can be removed while preserving uniqueness
mcqs.explain: A candidate key is a super key with no redundant attributes (minimal).

mcqs.q: An alternate key is:
options: A super key with extra attributes
A candidate key not chosen as the primary key
mcqs.explain: Among several candidate keys, the ones not selected as primary are alternate keys.

mcqs.q: A primary key, unlike other candidate keys, must:
options: Not be NULL and is the chosen main identifier
mcqs.explain: The primary key is the chosen candidate key and enforces non-null uniqueness.

u:core-dbms-12-foreign-keys-and-referent.title: Foreign keys and referential integrity
u:core-dbms-12-foreign-keys-and-referent.summary: A column that references another table's key, kept valid by referential integrity rules.

blocks.text: A **foreign key (FK)** is an attribute in one table that references the **primary key** of another (or the same) table, modelling a relationship. **Referential integrity** requires that every FK value either matches an existing PK value or is NULL.
On delete/update actions

headers: Effect when the referenced row is deleted/updated
rows: Reject the operation if references exist
Set the FK to a default value

blocks.text: Referential integrity prevents 'orphan' rows — an order referencing a customer that doesn't exist. The referential action (CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT) defines what happens to children when the parent changes.

mcqs.q: Referential integrity guarantees that a foreign key value:
options: Matches an existing primary key value or is NULL
mcqs.explain: An FK must reference an existing PK (or be NULL), preventing orphan references.

mcqs.q: ON DELETE CASCADE means when a referenced (parent) row is deleted:
options: The referencing (child) rows are deleted too
The FK is set to a default
mcqs.explain: CASCADE propagates the delete to the child rows that reference the parent.

mcqs.q: A foreign key models:
options: A relationship linking a row to another table's primary key
mcqs.explain: The FK expresses a relationship by referencing another table's primary key.

u:core-dbms-13-entity-and-referential-in.title: Entity and referential integrity constraints
u:core-dbms-13-entity-and-referential-in.summary: Two fundamental relational rules: primary keys can't be NULL, and foreign keys must be valid.

blocks.text: The relational model enforces two built-in integrity constraints.

items: **Entity integrity** — no part of a primary key may be NULL (a row must be identifiable). Also implies PK uniqueness.
**Referential integrity** — a foreign key must reference an existing primary-key value or be entirely NULL (no dangling references).

blocks.text: Other constraints layered on top: **domain constraints** (values from the correct domain), **key constraints** (uniqueness), and user-defined **check** constraints.
Entity integrity keeps every row identifiable (PK not null); referential integrity keeps relationships valid (FK points to something real). Together they are the backbone of relational correctness.

mcqs.q: Entity integrity requires that:
options: No attribute of a primary key is NULL
mcqs.explain: Entity integrity forbids NULLs in any part of the primary key so each row is identifiable.

mcqs.q: Referential integrity is violated when:
options: A foreign key references a non-existent primary-key value
mcqs.explain: A dangling foreign key (pointing to a missing PK) breaks referential integrity.

mcqs.q: A rule like 'salary > 0' is enforced by a:
mcqs.explain: Value-range rules are enforced by CHECK/domain constraints.

u:core-dbms-14-relational-algebra-operat.title: Relational algebra operators
u:core-dbms-14-relational-algebra-operat.summary: The procedural foundation of query languages: select, project, join, and set operations.

blocks.text: **Relational algebra** is a procedural query language — a set of operators that take relations and produce a relation. SQL is built on these.

rows: Every row of A paired with every row of B

blocks.text: Two to never mix up: **selection (σ)** filters ROWS; **projection (π)** filters COLUMNS. A join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection on the join condition.
Set operations (∪, ∩, −) require the relations to be union-compatible: same number of attributes with matching domains.

mcqs.q: The selection operator (σ) in relational algebra:
mcqs.explain: Selection (σ) filters tuples by a predicate — the WHERE of relational algebra.

mcqs.q: Projection (π) corresponds to which SQL clause?
mcqs.explain: Projection selects specific columns and removes duplicates, like SELECT of certain attributes.

mcqs.q: A join can be expressed as:
options: A Cartesian product followed by a selection on the join condition
mcqs.explain: A theta/natural join is a Cartesian product filtered by the matching condition.

u:core-dbms-15-tuple-and-domain-relation.title: Tuple and domain relational calculus
u:core-dbms-15-tuple-and-domain-relation.summary: The declarative counterpart to relational algebra — describe what you want, not how.

blocks.text: **Relational calculus** is a **non-procedural (declarative)** query language: you specify **what** the result should satisfy, not the steps to compute it (unlike procedural relational algebra).

items: **Tuple relational calculus (TRC)** — variables range over **tuples**: `{ t | P(t) }` (all tuples t for which predicate P is true).
**Domain relational calculus (DRC)** — variables range over **attribute domains** (individual values).
Both use quantifiers ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).

blocks.text: Algebra = how (procedural, operator steps); calculus = what (declarative, a logical condition). They are equivalent in expressive power for safe queries — the basis of SQL being declarative.
Calculus expressions must be 'safe' (produce a finite result); an unrestricted formula like {t | not R(t)} could be infinite.

mcqs.q: Relational calculus is characterised as:
mcqs.explain: Calculus specifies the properties of the desired result rather than the steps to compute it.

mcqs.q: In tuple relational calculus, variables range over:
mcqs.explain: TRC variables represent whole tuples; DRC variables represent domain values.

mcqs.q: Relational algebra and (safe) relational calculus are:
mcqs.explain: They have equivalent expressive power for safe queries, underpinning SQL.
